title: General Introduction, in modern English
label: The Workshop's modern English, machine-assisted: drafted with an AI model (Claude) and not yet checked by a scholar. Taylor's own words are under every paragraph.
about: A modern English version of Thomas Taylor's General Introduction to the Philosophy and Writings of Plato (1804), written for the Workshop, because none exists. It is made from Taylor's English, paragraph by paragraph: every idea is kept, the long sentences are broken into short ones, and old words are replaced by today's (the key words always the same way, linked to the Term tab). Taylor's Latin names of the gods are given in Greek (Zeus for Jupiter). The quotations he translates (Proclus, Damascius, Simplicius, Plato) are modernised from his English, not translated afresh from the Greek. His footnotes are left as he printed them, under his own words. The sections and their summaries are the Workshop's; Taylor's text has no headings. A flag marks a place that is hard, or where Taylor states as fact what is disputed, with his words and the reason.

sections.title: What philosophy is, and what this Introduction sets out to do
sections.summary: Taylor opens with Hierocles' definition: philosophy cleans the soul of the passions and the body's pull, and makes it like God again. Plato, he says, is the first and greatest guide to this philosophy, and every other school is true only so far as it agrees with him. He will first set out Plato's main teachings, which no one has explained for over a thousand years.

sections.title: The first principle, and the climb to what is beyond words
sections.summary: Plato's highest God, the One or the Good, is above soul, intellect and even being, and so nothing can be said of it. Taylor follows Damascius up a ladder of things, from bodies to nature, soul, intellect and being, showing that each one needs something higher, until we reach the One, and then something beyond even the One, before which we can only be silent.

sections.title: The gods who come first from the One
sections.summary: Straight from the One come many divine unities, the henads, which Taylor identifies with the gods. Taylor argues from the Republic's image of the sun, and from Simplicius, that the One gives rise first to things like itself. The gods exist in their own right and produce themselves, and from them come, in order, being, life, intellect and soul. The One does not make the world directly, not from weakness, but because it is too high; the world is made through the gods.

sections.title: How Plato teaches about the gods: inspiration, argument, symbols and images
sections.summary: Following Proclus, Taylor sets out four ways Plato speaks of the gods: as one inspired, by rigorous argument, through symbols and myths, and through images such as mathematics. He explains why the ancients used myths, how a philosopher's myth differs from a poet's, and which dialogues hold most of Plato's theology. Proclus answers an objector by naming the Parmenides as the one dialogue that holds the whole of it.

sections.title: The Forms
sections.summary: Plato's next great teaching is the Forms, the patterns of things. Taylor follows Syrianus: the Forms are not words, ideas in our heads, or general notions drawn from things we see, but real, simple, unchanging beings in the divine intellect. They are at once makers, patterns and ends of all things. Our souls hold images of them, which is why learning is recollection.

sections.title: The world: eternal, alive and divine
sections.summary: From the world of Forms the visible world flows out for ever, as a shadow from the body that casts it. Taylor argues that a maker who makes by power alone makes something that lasts as long as he does, so the world has no beginning in time. Taken as body it is always passing away, but taken as alive with a divine soul it is a blessed god, a whole of wholes, and each of its great parts is a world with its own unity, intellect, soul and body.

sections.title: The human being: intellect, reason, opinion, imagination and body
sections.summary: A human being holds in small and in part everything the world holds as a whole. Taylor sets out Plato's map of the soul: at the top, our intellect; then discursive reason, which reasons from first principles; then opinion; then imagination, anger and desire, and the senses. The soul is joined to the body through two finer "vehicles," and it holds in itself images of everything above it and patterns of everything below it.

sections.title: The soul's fall, the Cave, and the way back
sections.summary: Our souls come down into bodies and go back up again, in endless cycles. On earth the soul is in exile, like the prisoners in Plato's Cave who see only shadows. The way back is by the virtues that purify us from the passions and the virtues that contemplate truth; by these we become like God and, after death, go home to our star. Since the soul holds all knowledge within it, learning is recollection, and mathematics and dialectic wake that knowledge up.

sections.title: Providence, fate and free choice
sections.summary: Taylor ends his outline of Plato's teachings with providence and fate. Providence is God himself, the source of all good, and rules over everything. Fate is the life of nature that links bodies together in time, and rules only bodies. The rational soul is above fate when it lives by reason and below it when it gives in to the body. Our free choice sits between the gods, who choose only the true good, and the animals, who follow only what seems good.

sections.title: Why this philosophy was lost, and what Taylor thinks of the moderns
sections.summary: Taylor turns on his own age. The paths he has walked have been empty since the emperor Justinian closed the schools. People who trust only the senses and experiment will find all this a dream. He attacks the experimental science of his day, defends his reliance on the later Platonists, and explains why their reading of Plato should be preferred to modern ones.

sections.title: The kinds of dialogue, their parts and their style
sections.summary: Taylor, using Floyer Sydenham's outline, sorts the dialogues by how they teach (questioning or teaching outright), by their outward form (acted, narrated or mixed), and by their subject. He defends Plato's openings, digressions and grand style as serving the aim of each dialogue, and says even those who never reach their depths are helped by them.

sections.title: Taylor's order of the dialogues, and his translation
sections.summary: Taylor explains the order in which he prints the dialogues, starting from those that are "wholes," and explains his translation: which dialogues Sydenham translated, what he used of Spens, Dacier, Ficino and the editors, why he translates word for word, and which unpublished Greek commentaries he copied by hand for his notes. He ends by hoping his work will help bring the true philosophy back.

sections.title: Who can read Plato, and the Life that follows
sections.summary: Knowing Greek is not enough to understand Plato. Taylor describes the reader he hopes for: good by nature, eager for wisdom, trained in mathematics, and willing to spend years in hard thought. He warns off those who want wisdom cheaply, and ends by explaining why he prints Olympiodorus' Life of Plato before the dialogues.

paragraphs.modern: "Philosophy," says Hierocles, "purifies and perfects human life. It purifies us from the unreason of matter and from the mortal body. It perfects us by giving back the happiness that is properly ours, and by lifting us again into the likeness of God. These two tasks belong to Virtue and to Truth. Virtue removes the excess of the passions. Truth brings the divine form to those who are naturally fit to receive it."

Philosophy in this sense is like a pyramid of light. Its base is the rational soul of a human being, with the natural, undistorted ideas the soul has of itself. Its peak is God. Of this noble and divine philosophy Plato can rightly be called the first leader and the chief priest. Through him it first shone out, like the hidden light in the inmost shrine of a temple, with a deep and holy brightness. It can truly be said that this philosophy is the greatest good a human being can share in. If it cleans us of the stains of the passions and makes us like God, it gives us the happiness that belongs to our nature. From this it is easy to see why it stands above all other philosophies. Where they oppose it, they are wrong. So far as they contain real knowledge, they are related to it. At best they are small streams flowing from this great ocean of truth.

The main aim of this Introduction is to show four things: that Plato's philosophy really does stand above the others; that nothing equals its dignity and height; that everything which raises a human being comes from it; and that it rests on principles which time cannot erase and clever arguments cannot overturn.

To do this, I will first give the reader an outline of the main teachings of Plato's philosophy. This is a new and difficult task. Its author has to walk paths that no one has walked for more than a thousand years, and to bring to light truths that have been hidden all that time in Greek books. So the reader should not be surprised that the paths are lonely, or that the things seen along the way are strange. Perhaps the reader will happily remember having travelled this road before, that the views were once familiar, and that the country being crossed is home. At least, if the reader's sight is weak and memory dull (for these things can be seen only by the sharpest eyes), and if the time away from them has been sadly long, let the reader pray to the power of wisdom,

to clear the mist of mortal life from the eyes,
so that God and man can both be clearly seen.
(Homer, Iliad 5.127; Taylor gives the Greek beside his verse.)
Let us also ask the help of that same power of light, and begin the lonely journey.

Of all Plato's teachings, his teaching on the first principle of things rises as far above the teachings of other schools as that highest cause rises above all other causes. For Plato, the highest God, whom he calls the Good in the Republic and the One in the Parmenides, is not only above soul and intellect. It is above being itself. Anything that can be known in any way, or that anything can be said about, must belong to the whole of things. But the first cause is above all things. So Plato rightly says that it is completely beyond words. That is why the first hypothesis of his Parmenides, which denies everything of this great principle, ends like this:

"So the One is not in any way. So it seems. Then it is not even in such a way as to be one. For then it would be a being, and would share in being. But, as it seems, the One neither is one nor is, if we may trust this kind of reasoning. It seems so. Can anything belong to, or be said of, what is not? How could it? Then no name belongs to it, and no account, no knowledge, no perception and no opinion. It seems not. So it cannot be named, or spoken of, or held in opinion, or known, or perceived by any being. So it seems."

Notice that this conclusion, that the highest principle is completely beyond words and beyond thought, is reached by a rigorous series of denials. Not only all perceptible things and all things of intellect are denied of it, but even the things closest to it, its first and most divine offspring. What marks Plato's philosophy off from the others is that every part of it bears the stamp of real knowledge. Ordinary people do say that God is beyond words. But they do not know it with real understanding. So their belief is only a vague, confused sense of the highest of all truths. It is like something seen between sleeping and waking, like the land of the Phaeacians as Odysseus saw it, sailing home,

which lay before him, dim and huge,
like a wide shield on the misty sea.

In short, an untrained sense that God is beyond words is like this. A man looks up at the sky and says that its highest point is higher than the tallest tree, and so cannot be measured. But to see this with real knowledge is like the astronomer's view of the sky. Because the astronomer knows the heights of everything between us and that point, he knows for certain that it rises not only above the tallest tree, but above the top of the air and the upper air, above the moon, and even above the sun.

So let us ask what the climb to the inexpressible is, and how Plato makes it, starting from the lowest things. As our guide in this hard inquiry we take Damascius, a deep and searching thinker. Let our argument also apply to the other principles, and to the things that come from them, down to the last. Let us start from what is fully expressible and known to the senses, climb to what is beyond words, and there, in silence, as in a harbour, lay down what the search for truth has brought forth about it. We take this axiom as a safe vehicle for the journey from here to there: what is in need of nothing comes, by nature, before what is in need. What needs another thing must serve the thing it needs. If two things each need the other, in different ways, neither of them is the principle. Being in need of nothing is what suits a true principle best. If it needed anything, it would not be the principle in that respect. But the principle must be just this: the principle and nothing else. So being in need of nothing belongs to it, and we must not admit that anything comes before it. Yet we would have to admit that, if it had any link with what is in need.

Let us begin, then, with a body: something extended in three dimensions, with qualities. This is the first thing we can speak of, and it is perceptible. Is this the principle of things? But it is two things: the body, and the quality that is in the body as in a subject. Which of the two comes first by nature? Both need their own parts, and a quality, being in a subject, also needs that subject. Shall we say, then, that the body itself is the principle and the first being? That is impossible. First, a principle receives nothing from what comes after it. But a body, we say, receives quality. So quality, and the body's having quality, do not come from the body; quality is present in the body as something other than it. Second, a body can be divided in every way. Its parts need one another, and the whole needs all its parts. Since it is in need, and is completed by things that are in need, it cannot be wholly in need of nothing.

Again, if a body is not one thing but something made one, it needs, as Plato says, a one that holds it together. A body as such is also general and shapeless, a kind of matter. So it needs ordering and a form, so as to be not just body, but a body of a particular kind: a fiery body or an earthy one, a body shaped and clothed with a particular quality. The things added to it complete it and give it order. Is what is added the principle, then? That is impossible too. A quality does not stay in itself or exist on its own; it is in a subject, and it needs that subject. Someone might say that the body is not a subject, but one of the elements in each thing, as "animal" is an element in both horse and man. Even so, each needs the other: the subject and what is in the subject, or rather the common element ("animal") and the special features ("rational", "non-rational"). Elements always need one another, and what is made of elements needs the elements. In short, this perceptible thing that is so plain to us is not a body, for a body by itself does not act on the senses. Nor is it a quality, for a quality has no size the senses can take in. What the eye sees is neither body nor colour, but a coloured body, colour made bodily. In general, what is perceptible, a body with a particular quality, is what acts on the senses. So it is clear that what stirs the senses has something bodiless in it. If it were only body, it would not yet be perceived. So body needs the bodiless, and the bodiless needs body, since something bodiless is not perceptible by itself. Yet the two differ, because each has its own powers, and neither exists before the other. They are elements of one perceptible thing, and are present in each other. One gives extension to what has none; the other gives what is shapeless a perceptible variety and a form. Third, the two together are not the principle either, for they are not in need of nothing. They need their own elements, and they need something to bring them together into one form. Body cannot do this, for by itself it is powerless. Nor can quality, for it cannot exist apart from the body it is in, or with which it exists. So either the compound makes itself, which is impossible, because it does not gather into itself but is scattered in many ways; or it is not made by itself, and there is some other principle before it.

Suppose, then, that the principle is what we call nature: a source of motion and rest in what moves and rests, belonging to it in its own right and not by accident. Nature is simpler than bodies, and it shapes compound forms. But if nature is in the things it makes, and does not exist apart from them or before them, but needs them in order to be, it will not be in need of nothing. It does have something above them: the power to shape and make them. Yet it exists together with them and cannot be separated from them. When they exist, it exists; when they do not, it does not. This is because it leans wholly towards them, and cannot keep to what is its own. The powers of growth, nourishment and reproduction, and nature, which comes before these three, are not wholly bodiless. Nature is almost a quality of body. It differs from body only in that it lets the compound be moved and rest from within. The perceptible quality gives what appears in matter and what meets the senses. The body gives extension in every direction. Nature gives a natural activity that works from within, whether moving the thing from place to place, or feeding it, making it grow and making it produce its like. But nature cannot be separated from its subject, and it is in need. So it cannot be the principle, since it needs what is below it. It would not be strange for a principle to need the principle above it. It would be strange for it to need the things after it, of which it is supposed to be the principle.

In the same way we can show that the principle cannot be the non-rational soul, whether the soul that perceives or the soul that desires. It may seem to have something separate from the body, since it has drives and a kind of knowing. Yet it is tied to the body and has something that cannot be separated from it. It cannot turn back to itself; its activity is mixed with its subject. Its being is plainly of this kind. If it were set free and independent, it would show some activity of its own. It would not always be turned to the body; sometimes it would turn to itself. Or, even if it were always turned to the body, it would still judge and examine itself. Now the activities of most people, although they deal with outward things, still show something separate in them. People consider how to go about things, and see that they must deliberate in order to get or undergo what seems good, or to avoid its opposite. But the drives of other animals are simple and automatic. They move together with the sense organs, and they need only the senses to get pleasure from perceptible things and avoid pain. Since the body shares in pleasure and pain, and is affected by them, it is clear that the soul's activities here are carried out mixed with bodies. They are not purely activities of soul, but also of body. Perception belongs to the living body, or to the soul made bodily, even though in perception the soul's character outweighs the body's, just as in bodies the body's character rules in extension and existence. So the non-rational soul, which has its being in something other than itself, needs what is below it, and nothing of that kind can be the principle.

Before this kind of being we find a form that is separate from any subject and turns back to itself. This is the rational nature. Our soul is in charge of its own activities and corrects itself. That could not happen unless it turned back to itself, and it could not turn back to itself unless its being were separate. So it does not need what is below it. Shall we say, then, that it is the most perfect principle? But it does not carry out all its activities at once; it always lacks most of them. A principle must lack nothing, yet the rational nature is a being that lacks its own activities. Someone may reply that the soul is an eternal being, with activities of its own that never fail and always go with its being, since it moves itself and is always alive; so it lacks nothing and is the principle. Our answer is that the whole soul is one form and one nature, in part lacking nothing and in part in need. The principle lacks nothing at all. So soul, which acts in changing ways, is not the true principle. There must be something before it that does not change in any way: in nature, in life, in knowledge, and in all its powers and activities. Such is what we call an eternal, unchanging being, and such is the highly honoured intellect. Aristotle climbed as far as intellect and thought he had found the first principle. For what could be lacking to something that holds all its fullness (plērōmata) within itself, and that nothing can be added to or taken from? Yet is intellect, too, not one and many, a whole with parts, holding first, middle and last things within itself? Its lower contents need the higher, the higher need the lower, and the whole needs the parts. Related things need each other, and the first need the last, for the same reason: nothing is "first" on its own. Further, the one in intellect needs the many, because it exists in the many. Or we may say that this one gathers the many together, but not by itself, only together with them. So there is much need in this principle. Intellect produces within itself its own contents, which together complete the whole. So it needs itself: what is produced needs what produces it, and what produces needs what is produced, for the whole to be complete, since the whole produces itself. Again, intellect thinks and is thought. It is both the thinker of itself and the object of its own thought, and it is both together. So the side of intellect that thinks needs the intelligible side, the object of its thought, as the thing it longs for; and the intelligible side needs the thinking side, because it wants to be the object of that thinking. Each needs the other, since having something always goes with having needed it, just as the world is always joined to matter. So some need is part of the very being of intellect, and it cannot be the true principle. Shall we turn next to the simplest of beings, which Plato calls "the one being" (hen on)? There is no division in it at all, no multitude, no order, no doubleness, no turning back on itself. What need could there be in something perfectly one, and above all what need of anything lower? So the great Parmenides climbed to this safest principle, the being that is least in need. But here we must attend to Plato's thought: what is made one is not the One itself, but something that has received oneness from it. If so, it plainly comes after the One, since it is taken to be the united and not the One itself. Further, if being is made of the elements limit and the unlimited, as the Philebus shows, where Plato calls it "the mixture," then it needs its elements. Again, if the idea of being is different from the idea of being united, and the whole is both united and being, the two need each other, and the whole called "one being" needs both. And although the one in it is better than being, it still needs being for there to be a one being. If being comes on top of the one, as form comes on top of what is mixed and united (as "man" comes on top of the combination rational-mortal-animal), then the one also will need being. And if, to speak more exactly, there are two "ones," one the cause of the mixture and existing before being, the other giving being its right order, even so need does not leave this nature entirely. After all these, it may be said that the One will be wholly in need of nothing. It does not need what comes after it in order to exist, since the true One is separate by itself from all things. It does not need anything lower or higher within itself, for there is nothing in it but itself. Nor does it need itself. It is one, because it has no doubleness towards itself; we must not even speak of the true One as related to itself, since it is perfectly simple. So it is the least needy of all things. Therefore it is the principle and cause of all, and the first of all things. But if these qualities belong to it, it will not be the One. Or may we say that all things are in the One in the manner of the One? That these qualities, and all the others we say of it, are in it: the simplest, the best, the most powerful, the preserver of all things, the Good itself? But if these things are true of the One, then it also needs the things after it, in the very respects we add to it. A principle is, and is called, the principle of the things that come from it; a cause is the cause of its effects; the first is first of the things ranked after it. Again, "simplest" means surpassing other things; "most powerful" means having power over what is subject to it; "the Good," "the desirable" and "the preserver" are so called in relation to the things it benefits, preserves, and is desired by. If it is said to be all things because it holds all things beforehand within itself, it will be so only as the One. It will be the one cause of all things, before all, and it will be this and nothing else, as the One. So far as it is the One alone, it lacks nothing. So far as it lacks nothing, it is the first principle and firm root of all principles. But so far as it is the principle and first cause of all things, set up as what all things desire, it seems in some way to need the things it is related to. So it has, if we may say so, a last trace of need, just as matter, at the other end, has a last echo of needing nothing, a very faint and weak imprint of the One. Here language seems to turn upside down. So far as it is the One, it lacks nothing, for the principle turned out to be what is one and least in need. Yet so far as it is the One, it is also the principle. So as the One it lacks nothing, but as the principle it is in need. So in the same thing it both lacks nothing and needs, though not in the same respect. In being what it is, it lacks nothing. In producing other things and holding them within itself, it needs. This is the special character of the One: it is both needless and needy, as the One. Not that it is each of these, in the way we divide it when we speak of it; it is one alone, and as such it is both all other things and the needy. How could it fail to be needy, so far as it is the One, just as it is all the other things that come from it? For need also is one of "all things." So we must look for something else, which has no need of any kind. But of such a thing we cannot truly say that it is the principle. We cannot even say that it is "least in need," though that seems the most reverent thing we could say, because that phrase means rising above need and being free of it. We do not think it right to call it even "wholly free." Instead, the truest rule for our thought in this inquiry is this: it cannot be grasped in any way, and we must keep perfect silence about it. Not even this rule says anything about it; it rejoices in saying nothing, and in this way honours that vast unknown. This, then, is the way up to what is called the First, or rather to what lies beyond everything that can be thought or supposed.

There is also a second way. It does not put the needless before the needy. Instead it shows that whatever needs something better comes after that better thing. Everywhere, what exists potentially comes after what exists actually. In order to become actual, and not remain a mere possibility to no purpose, it needs something that is already actual. The better never grows out of the worse. Let us lay this down first, as our common, undistorted ideas tell us. Matter, then, has before it the form that is in matter, because all matter is form in potential. This is true of first matter, which has no form at all, and of second matter, which is body without quality, mere extension in three dimensions. Those who first studied perceptible things probably looked at this second matter, since at first it seemed that only bodies exist. The fact that something is common to the different elements persuaded them that there is a body without quality. But among such bodies, some have their ruling principle inside them, while others, such as things made by art, have it outside. So, besides quality, we must look to nature, which is better than qualities and stands before them as their cause, as art stands before the things it makes. Of the things ruled from within, some seem only to exist, while others are fed, grow, and produce their like. So there is another cause before the nature just mentioned: the power of plant life itself. Plainly, everything that comes to be in a body as in a subject is bodiless in itself, though it becomes bodily by sharing in what it is in. So these things are said to be material, and are material, because of what they undergo from matter. Qualities, and natures still more, and plant life even more, keep something bodiless in them. But perception shows another, plainer kind of life, belonging to beings that move by impulse from place to place. This must be placed before plant life as a truer principle, which supplies a better form: the self-moving animal, which by nature comes before plants rooted in the earth. Yet the animal does not strictly move itself. The whole of it does not move the whole of it: one part moves, and another part is moved. So it only seems to move itself. Before it, then, there must be something that truly moves itself, which moves and is moved as a whole, so that the apparent self-mover may be its image. The soul that moves the body must be seen as a truer self-moving being. But the soul is of two kinds, rational and non-rational. That there is a rational soul is clear. Does not everyone have some awareness of himself, clearer or dimmer, when he turns to himself in attending to and examining himself, and in noticing his own life and knowledge? A being that can do this, and can gather universals by reasoning, is rightly called rational. The non-rational soul, although it does not seem to examine these things and reason with itself, still moves bodies from place to place, having first been moved by itself; for at different times it has different impulses. Does it, then, move itself from one impulse to another? Or is it moved by something else, for example by the whole rational soul of the universe? It would be absurd to say that the activities of each non-rational soul are not its own, but belong to a more divine soul, since they are countless and mixed with much that is base and imperfect. That would be the same as saying that non-rational activities are the activities of the rational soul. I leave aside the absurdity of supposing that a whole being does not produce its own activities. If the non-rational soul is a being, it will have activities of its own, not given from elsewhere but coming from itself. So the non-rational soul will also move itself, at different times, to different impulses. But if it moves itself, it will turn back to itself. And if so, it will exist separately and will not be in a subject. Then it is rational, if it looks at itself, since in turning to itself it surveys itself. But when it reaches out to outward things, it looks at those things, or rather at coloured bodies, and does not see itself, because sight itself is neither a body nor coloured. So it does not turn back to itself. The same is true of every other non-rational power. Imagination does not form a picture of itself, but of something perceptible, such as a coloured body. Non-rational desire does not desire itself, but reaches for something desirable, such as honour, pleasure or wealth. So it does not move itself.

Someone may see that animals act in ways that look rational, and conclude that they too share in the first self-mover, and so have a soul that turns back to itself. We may grant that they too are rational natures. But they are not rational in their essence, only by sharing, and very dimly; just as the rational soul may be called "of intellect" by sharing, because it always puts forward common ideas without distorting them. We should note that at the two ends are what can be wholly separate, such as the rational form, and what cannot be separated at all, such as a bodily quality. Between them is nature, which leans towards the inseparable but has a little image of the separable. And there is the non-rational soul, which leans towards the separable, since in some way it seems to exist by itself apart from a subject. So it is unclear whether it moves itself or is moved by another. It has a strong trace of self-motion, but not true self-motion, which turns back to itself and is therefore wholly separate from a subject. The plant soul also stands in a kind of middle position. That is why some of the ancients thought it was a soul, and others thought it was nature.

Let us go back to our question. How can a self-mover of this kind, mixed with what is moved by another, be the first principle of things? It does not exist from itself, nor does it really complete itself. It needs another nature both to exist and to be completed, and before it is what truly moves itself. Is what truly moves itself the principle, then, and does it need no form better than itself? Or does not what moves always come by nature before what is moved? And does not every form that is pure of its opposite exist by itself before the form that is mixed with it? And is not the pure the cause of the mixed? Whatever has its being joined with another also has its activity mixed with that other. So a self-mover makes itself, but in doing so it is both moving and moved; it is not made a mover only, for it is not only that. But every form, in its first existence, is always alone. So there will be something that only moves, without being moved. It would be absurd if there were something that is only moved, such as body, but nothing that only moves, before both the self-mover and what is only moved. Plainly there must be, since it will be better; and the self-mover, so far as it moves itself, is better than it is so far as it is moved. So the being that moves without being moved must be first, and what is moved without moving is third. In between is the self-mover, which, we say, needs the unmoved mover in order to become a mover. In short, so far as it is moved, it does not stay still; and so far as it moves, it must remain a mover. Where, then, does it get the power to stay? From itself it gets either the power to be moved only, or the power to stay and be moved at once, as a whole and in the same respect. Where does it get the simple power to stay? Surely from what simply stays. And that is an unmoving cause. So we must place the unmoving before the self-moving. Is the unmoving, then, the true principle? How could it be? The unmoving holds a multitude without motion, just as the self-mover holds one with motion. And an unmoving division must come before a self-moving division. So the unmoving is at once one and many, at once united and divided; and such a nature is called intellect. Clearly, the united in intellect comes by nature before the divided, and is more honoured, since division always needs union, but union does not need division. But intellect does not have the united pure from its opposite. The form that belongs to intellect is joined in its whole being with the divided. So what is united in some respect needs what is simply united. What exists with another needs what exists by itself, and what has something by sharing needs what has it by its own being. Intellect, existing from itself, produces itself as both united and divided, and so it exists as both. It is produced, then, from what is simply united and only united. So before what has forms is what has no outline and is not divided into forms. This is what we call the united, and what the wise men of old called being: it holds a multitude drawn together into one, existing before the many.

Having come this far, let us stop for a while and consider whether being is the principle of all things that we are looking for. What is there that does not share in being? But if being is what is made one, will it not come after the One, becoming united by sharing in the One? In short, if we think of the One as different from being, and if being comes before the One, then being will not share in the One. Then it will be many only, an endless number of endless numbers. But if the One is with being, and being with the One, either they are on the same level or set apart from each other, and then there will be two principles and the same absurdity follows. Or they share in each other, and they will be two elements. Or they are parts of something else made from both. And then what brings them into union? If the One unites being to itself (for someone may say this), then the One acts before being, in order to call being out and turn it towards itself. So the One will exist by itself, complete in itself, before being. Again, the simpler always comes before the more compound. If the two are equally simple, there will be either two principles or one made of the two, and that would be a compound. So before it is the simple and wholly uncompounded, which must be either one or not one. If not one, it must be either many or nothing. If "nothing" means the wholly empty, it means something idle. If it means the secret and inexpressible, then it will not even be the simple. In short, we cannot think of any principle simpler than the One. So the One comes before being in every way. This, then, is the principle of all things, and Plato, coming back to it, needed no other principle in his arguments. For the inexpressible, where our climb ends, is not the principle of reasoning, or knowledge, or living things, or beings, or henads, but simply of all things, and is placed above every idea and every guess we can form. So Plato says nothing about it. He makes his denials of all other things except the One, starting from the One. In the end he denies that the One is, but he does not deny the One. He even denies the denial, but not the One. He denies name and idea, all knowledge, and, what more can be said, wholeness itself and every being. Let there be the united and the single, and, if you like, the two principles, limit and the unlimited. Yet Plato never in any way denies the One that is beyond all these. So in the Sophist he treats it as the One before being, and in the Republic as the Good beyond all being; but all the same the One alone is left. Is it, then, known and expressible, or unknown and inexpressible? Or is it in one way these and in another way not? For by denying that it can be spoken of, someone may say, we affirm that it is inexpressible. Again, by the simplicity of knowing it will be known or guessed at, but by composition it is wholly unknown. So it will not be grasped by denial either. In short, so far as it is admitted to be one, it is ranked with the other things that can be posited, since it is the summit of things that are posited. Yet there is much in it that is inexpressible and unknown, unranked and beyond position; but these come with an image of their opposites, and the first are better than the second. Everywhere, pure things come before their opposites, and the unmixed before the mixed. Either the better things are in the One in its own being, and then their opposites will in some way be there too; or they are in it by sharing, and come from something that is first of this kind. So before the One is what is simply and wholly inexpressible, beyond position, unranked, and impossible to grasp. Our argument hurries up to it by the clearest signs, leaving out none of the natures between the first of things and the last.
