flags.why: Damascius' view that there is something "beyond" even the One is his own, and the later Platonists did not all accept it; Taylor follows him here.

paragraphs.modern: This, then, is the climb to the highest God in Plato's theology. It keeps in all reverence his inexpressible separateness from all things, and his height, which no act of knowing can enclose. At the same time it opens the paths that lead up to him, and kindles that bright summit of the soul by which she is joined to the One who cannot be grasped.

From this truly inexpressible principle, which is beyond all being, power and activity, there comes at once, according to Plato, a multitude of divine natures. A reader who has understood what we have said already will grant that this must be so, and Plato fully proves it in the Parmenides, as an attentive reader will see from the notes on that dialogue. I add only this. The teaching rests on the highest and most rigorous ideas the human mind can reach, and it can be clearly shown to be Plato's own from the sixth book of the Republic. There he says, plainly and without doubt, that the Good, the inexpressible principle of things, is beyond being. And by comparing the sun to the Good he shows that truth and intelligence are in the intelligible world what light and sight are in the visible world. Light comes straight from the sun and has entirely the character of the sun. In the same way truth, the first offspring of the Good, must have the character of what is beyond being. Since the Good, for Plato, is the same as the One, as the Parmenides shows, the first offspring of the One will be the first offspring of the Good. But the first offspring of the One can only be henads. So we must conclude that for Plato the first offspring of the inexpressible principle are henads beyond being. They differ from their vast principle in this: the One is beyond being and inexpressible, with nothing added, while this divine multitude is shared in by the various orders of being, which hang from it and are produced by it. Because sharing links them to multitude, they must rank below the One.

flags.taylor: the immediate offspring of the one cannot be any thing else than unities
flags.why: That the "unities" (henads) are the gods is the teaching of Iamblichus and Proclus, read back into Plato; Plato does not say so in these words.

paragraphs.modern: Simplicius, in his commentary on Epictetus, says something on this subject that is both admirable and truly Platonic:

"The source and principle of all things is the Good. What all things desire, and reach towards, is the beginning and the end of all things. The Good also produces all things from itself, the first, the middle and the last. But the things it produces first and nearest to itself it makes like itself: from one goodness, many goodnesses; from one simplicity and unity above all others, many unities; from one principle, many principles. For the One, the principle, the Good and God are the same. God is the first and the cause of all things. And the first must also be the simplest, since whatever is compound and has multitude comes after the One. Multitude, and things that are not good, desire the Good as being above them. In short, whatever is not itself the principle comes from the principle.
"The principle of all things must also have the highest power, and all power. The greatness of power lies in producing all things from itself, and in bringing like things into being before unlike things. So the one principle produces, close to itself, many principles, many simplicities and many goodnesses. Since all things differ from one another and are multiplied by their own differences, each of these multitudes hangs from its own single principle. For example, all beautiful things, whatever and wherever they are, in souls or in bodies, hang from one source of beauty. So too whatever has proportion, whatever is true, and all principles, are in a way akin to the first principle, so far as they are principles, sources and goodnesses, each in its proper lower place and proportion. What the one principle is to all beings, each of the other principles is to the multitude that has its character. Since each multitude is marked by a certain difference, it cannot fail to reach towards its own principle, which shines one and the same form on all the members of that multitude. For the one leads every multitude, and every special character in the many comes to the many from the one.
"So all particular principles are set in the principle that is a whole, and are held in it, not spread out as a multitude, but as parts in the whole, as multitude in the one, as number in the monad. For this first principle is all things before all things. Many principles are multiplied around the one principle, and many goodnesses are set in the one goodness. Nor is it a principle like each of the others. Of these, one is the principle of beauty, another of proportion, another of truth, another of something else; but it is simply principle. Nor is it simply the principle of beings; it is the principle of principles. For the character of being a principle, like everything else, must not begin with multitude, but must be gathered into one monad as its summit, which is the principle of principles.
"So the things first produced by the first Good, being born together with it, do not fall away from goodness itself. They do not move or change, and they stay for ever in the same blessedness. Nor do they lack the Good, since they are goodnesses themselves. But all other natures, produced by the one Good and the many goodnesses, fall away from goodness itself and are not fixed without motion in the hyparxis of divine goodness. So they have the Good only by sharing in it."

This high teaching at once makes clear the meaning of the ancient Egyptian saying that God is all things. As Simplicius rightly says in the passage above, the first principle is all things before all things. That is, it holds all things as their cause, and this is the highest way of holding them. All things, as they exist in God as their cause, are far better than they are as effects that come out from him. So that great, all-embracing whole, the first principle, is said to be all things before all things, and "before" here means being above and apart. The monad and the centre of a circle, because they are simple, are images of this greatest principle. They also show clearly how it holds all things as their cause. All number may be seen as hidden in the monad, and the circle in its centre; and this hidden being is, in each, the same as being there as in a cause.

This idea of being in something as in a cause was not invented by the later Platonists. It is Plato's own teaching, as the Philebus shows, for there he says plainly that in Zeus a kingly intellect and a kingly soul exist as in their cause. Pherecydes of Syros, too, in his Hymn to Zeus, as Kircher quotes it (in his Oedipus Aegyptiacus), has these lines:

flags.taylor: as cited by Kercher (in Oedip. Egyptiac.)
flags.why: Taylor takes these lines from Athanasius Kircher, a seventeenth-century source; their claim to be by Pherecydes is very doubtful.

paragraphs.modern: These witnesses show well enough how old this high teaching is.

Here we must note something Damascius tells us. Almost all philosophers before Iamblichus said that there is one God beyond being, but that the other gods had being, and were made divine by light from the One. They also said that there are many henads beyond being, which are not complete in themselves, but are unions with God given to beings by the highest God. That this view does not agree with Plato's teaching is clear from his Parmenides, where he shows that the One is not "in itself." As we have noted from Proclus in the notes on that dialogue, whatever is its own cause and exists from itself is said to be "in itself." A producing power always holds, as cause, what it produces. So whatever produces itself must hold itself so far as it is the cause, and be held by itself so far as it is caused; it must be at once cause and effect, what holds and what is held. If, then, for Plato, being "in another" means being produced by another, better cause, being "in itself" must mean being self-begotten, produced by itself. If the One does not exist from itself, because it is above even this way of existing, and if there must be something that does exist from itself, then this must be the special mark of what comes straight from the inexpressible. And there must be something that exists from itself, for unless we admit this, nothing will be truly self-sufficient.

Besides, as Damascius rightly says, if something lower by nature, such as the human soul, is complete in itself, a divine soul will be so much more. If a soul is, so is intellect. If intellect is, so is life; if life, so is being; and if being, so are the henads above being. Being complete in itself, being self-sufficient, and being set in itself belong much more to higher natures than to lower ones. So if these are found in the lower, they will be found in the higher; I mean existing by itself and having its being in itself. Such are being and life, intellect, soul and body. Body does not exist from itself, but it does exist by itself. That is why it belongs to the class of substance, and is set against an attribute, which cannot exist apart from a subject.

So natures beyond being that exist from themselves are the first offspring of the One, if we may call them so. It would be better to call them inexpressible unfoldings into light from the inexpressible, for "offspring" implies a producing cause, and the One must be thought of as above this. From this divine multitude, complete in itself and producing itself, there comes, according to Plato, a series of natures complete in themselves: beings, lives, intellects and souls. In the last link of this bright chain Plato puts the human soul, which hangs next below the order of daemons. For this order, as he clearly says in the Symposium, "stands in the middle between the divine and the human, fills the space between, and binds all that has intelligence together." Here a reader who has not gone deep into Plato's philosophy will no doubt find it a complete paradox that anything should produce itself and yet come from a higher cause. The answer to this difficulty is as follows.

flags.taylor: and links together all intelligent nature
flags.why: Taylor's quotation adds to Plato. Symposium 202e says only that the daemonic fills the space between gods and humans, "so that the whole is bound together with itself."

paragraphs.modern: Producing by being, that is, the activity by which a nature produces something else just by being what it is, is the most perfect way of producing, since traces of it are found even in the lowest things. Fire gives heat simply by being fire, and snow gives cold. In short, this is the kind of producing in which the effect is, at a second level, what the cause is at the first level. Since this way of producing is the most perfect, it begins from the highest natures. So it belongs first to those powers that exist from themselves and come straight from the inexpressible, and from them it passes to all the following orders of beings. But because this activity is marked by being, it will differ in different producing causes. So from what stands at the summit of the self-existing natures, a series of self-existing beings will come. But the series will be, at a second level, what its cause is at the first; and the activity by which it produces itself will rank below the activity by which its cause produces it. For example, the rational soul both produces itself, since it moves itself, and is produced by intellect. But intellect produces it without change, and it produces itself step by step, since all its activities happen in time and with motion. So far as soul has intellect by sharing, it is produced by intellect; so far as it moves itself, it is produced by itself. In short, in everything that exists from itself, the summit of its nature is produced by a higher cause, but the unfolding of that summit is its own free activity. Through this it exists from itself and is complete in itself.
That the rational soul, so far as it is rational, produces itself can be clearly shown as follows.

Whatever can give something higher and better in any kind of thing can easily give what is lower and less good in the same kind. Now being well is admittedly higher and better than merely being. The rational soul gives itself well-being when it trains and perfects itself, and draws itself back from the body's infection. So it will also give itself being. And this is fitting. All divine natures, and all things that can give something to others in the first place, must begin this activity with themselves. The sun is a shining example of this great truth. It lights all things with its light, and it is itself light, and the source and origin of all brightness. So, since the soul gives life and motion to other things (which is why Aristotle calls an animal autokinēton, self-moved), it will much more, and much more first of all, give life and motion to itself.

From this great, high and rigorous teaching of Plato about the hidden principle of things and his first offspring, it follows that this inexpressible cause is not the direct maker of the universe. As I said in the Introduction to the Timaeus, this is not through any lack in him, but on the contrary through the height of his power. All things are indeed unfolded from him into light at once, in an inexpressible way. But divine intermediaries are needed to make the world. If the universe came directly from the inexpressible, then, as we said above, it too would be inexpressible at a second level. Since that is far from the case, it gets its direct existence chiefly from a god whose character is to make, whom Plato calls Zeus, in agreement with the theology of Orpheus. A thoughtful reader will readily see that this teaching does not lower the dignity of the Supreme; on the contrary, it raises it, and keeps fittingly the separate height of the inexpressible. So if we dare to praise him (and, as we have said, it is better to lay to rest in silence the soul's labour as it anxiously tries to search him out), we should praise him as the principle of principles and the source of all divinity, or, in the reverent words of the Egyptians, as "a darkness three times unknown." The reverence the great ancients paid to this vast principle deserves praise and imitation by all who come after. I have noted this already in the Introduction to the Parmenides. I add now only that, out of this deep and devout reverence for the first God, they did not even dare to give a name to the summit of the highest order of gods, the order called intelligible. So Proclus says, in his unpublished notes on the Cratylus:

flags.taylor: a deity of a fabricative characteristic, whom Plato calls Jupiter
flags.why: Taylor uses the Latin names of the gods (Jupiter for Zeus) throughout. The modern version uses the Greek names.

paragraphs.modern: "Not every kind of god has a name. Of the first God, who is beyond all things, Parmenides teaches us that he is inexpressible. And the first kinds of intelligible gods, who are united to the One and are called hidden, have much that is unknown and inexpressible. For what is fully expressible cannot be joined to what is fully inexpressible. The procession of intelligibles must end in this order, in which the first expressible thing exists, the first that is called by its own name. For there the first intelligible Forms, and the intellect-like nature of intelligibles, are unfolded into light. But the natures before this are silent and hidden, and are known only by intelligence. That is why the whole art of the sacred rites, working by theurgy, rises as far as this order. Orpheus also says that this is the first to be called by a name by the other gods, for the light that comes from it is known and named by the gods of intellect."
So Proclus speaks of the inexpressible principle of things with as much grandeur as devotion:

"Now, if ever, let us put away knowledge of many kinds, and quiet all the variety of our life, and in perfect stillness draw near to the cause of all things. For this, let not only opinion and imagination be at rest, and not only the passions that hold back our upward drive towards the First; let the air and the universe itself be still. Let all things carry us, with a calm power, into communion with the inexpressible. Standing there, beyond the intelligible (if there is anything of that kind in us), with eyes almost closed, as if worshipping the rising sun (for no being at all may look at him directly), let us gaze at the sun from which the light of the intelligible gods comes, rising, as the poets say, out of the bosom of the ocean. Then, coming down from this divine stillness into intellect, and from intellect using the reasonings of the soul, let us tell ourselves what the natures are from which, in this procession downwards, we shall think of the first God as set apart. Let us praise him, so to speak, not as founding the earth and the heavens, nor as giving being to souls and to the births of all living things; he did produce these, but among the last of things. Before these, let us praise him as bringing into light the whole kind of intelligible gods and gods of intellect, with all the gods above the world and in the world; as the God of all gods, the Unity of all unities, beyond the first inner shrines; as more inexpressible than all silence and more unknown than all being; holy among the holy, hidden in the intelligible gods."

Such is the devotion, and such the height and grandeur of thought, with which the Platonic philosophers speak of what is truly inexpressible in every way, when they dare to speak of it at all, reaching with the soul's inexpressible labour towards an inexpressible awareness of the One who cannot be grasped.

Out of this deep reverence for this most awesome nature, which, as the passages from Damascius note, led the oldest theologians, philosophers and poets to keep complete silence about it, came the great reverence the ancients paid even to the gods of the world, the gods on whom bodies depend. They saw these gods too as sharing in the nature of the inexpressible, as so many links in the truly golden chain of the divine. So in the Odyssey, when Odysseus and Telemachus are taking the weapons down from the walls of the palace on Ithaca, Athena goes before them with a golden lamp and fills the whole place with divine light:

and Pallas Athena went before them,
holding a golden lamp, and made a beautiful light.
(Homer, Odyssey 19.33-34, in Greek in Taylor.)
Telemachus sees it and says that surely one of the gods of heaven is present:

"Surely some god is here, one of those who hold the wide heaven."
(Odyssey 19.40, in Greek in Taylor.)
Odysseus answers: "Be silent. Hold back your intellect, and ask nothing." (That is: even stop thinking.)

flags.taylor: restrain your intellect (i.e. even cease to energize intellectually)
flags.why: Homer's words (kata son noon ischane) mean "keep it to yourself" or "hold it in your mind"; Taylor reads noos as intellect in the Platonists' sense.

paragraphs.modern:
"Be silent, keep it in your mind, and ask nothing."
(Odyssey 19.42, in Greek in Taylor.)

Finally, from all that has been said, it must be plain at once to anyone whose mind's eye is not completely blind that there is no trinity in Plato's theology at all like the Christian Trinity. For Plato's highest God, as we have shown at length from evidence that cannot be resisted, is so far from being one part of a triad of equal beings that he cannot be counted with anything at all. He is so wholly free of all multitude that he is beyond even being, and he rises so far above every relation and connection that language really breaks down about him, and knowledge turns back into ignorance. What the trinity in Plato's theology really is, which no doubt gave birth to the Christian one, will be clear to a thoughtful reader from the notes on the Parmenides and the passages from Damascius. So much for Plato's teaching on the principle of things and its first offspring. Its great importance will, I am sure, excuse the length of this discussion.

flags.taylor: which doubtless gave birth to the Christian
flags.why: This is Taylor's own opinion, stated without evidence; historians do not accept that the Christian Trinity came from a Platonic trinity in this way.

paragraphs.modern: Next, with Proclus and Olympiodorus as our guides, let us consider how Plato teaches the hidden ideas about divine natures. He does not seem to use the same way of teaching about them everywhere. Sometimes he unfolds the truth about them in a state of divine inspiration, and at other times by dialectic. Sometimes he hints at their inexpressible characters through symbols, and at other times he works back to them from images and finds in them the first causes of all things. In the Phaedrus, plainly inspired, having traded human intelligence for something better, divine madness, he reveals many hidden teachings about the gods of intellect, the gods who are free of the world, and the gods of the world. But in the Sophist, arguing dialectically about being, and about the One that exists above beings, and raising difficulties against older philosophers, he shows how all beings hang from their cause, the first being. And he shows that being itself shares in the unity that is apart from all things: it is a one that has been made one, not the One itself; it is under the One and united to it, but it is not what is one in the first place. In the same way, in the Parmenides, he sets out dialectically how being comes out from the One, through the first hypothesis of that dialogue, and this, as he says there, by the most perfect kind of division in this method. Again, in the Gorgias he tells the myth of the three makers and how they divided the world among them. In the Symposium he speaks of the union that love brings, and in the Protagoras of how the gods gave out their gifts to mortal animals. Here he hides the truth about divine natures in symbols, and shows his mind only by hints, to his truest readers.

flags.taylor: the three fabricators, and their demiurgic allotment
flags.why: This is Proclus' reading of the myth at Gorgias 523a, where Zeus, Poseidon and Pluto divide the rule of the world; Plato does not call them "makers."

paragraphs.modern: Then there is the teaching given through mathematics, and the treatment of divine things through discussions of ethics or of nature. Much of this can be seen in the Timaeus, much in the Statesman, and much is scattered in other dialogues. Here too the method will be clear to those who want to know divine things through images. For example, the Statesman gives a picture of the making that goes on in the heavens. The shapes of the five elements in the Timaeus, set out in geometrical proportions, are images of the characters of the gods who rule over the parts of the universe. And the divisions of the soul's being in that dialogue are a picture of the whole orders of the gods. We may add that Plato designs constitutions of cities to resemble divine natures, and furnishes them from the whole world and the powers in it. All these, through the likeness of mortal things to divine ones, show us in images the processions, orders and makings of the divine. These, then, are the ways of teaching theology that Plato uses.

"Those who speak of divine things by hints," says Proclus, "speak either in symbols and myths, or through images. And of those who state their thoughts openly, some build their accounts on knowledge, and others on inspiration from the gods. Whoever wants to show divine things through symbols is Orphic, and in short agrees with those who write myths about the gods. Whoever does it through images is Pythagorean. The Pythagoreans invented mathematics to help us recollect divine things, and they try to climb up to them through these as images. According to their historians, they assigned both numbers and figures to the gods. But the inspired kind of writer, who sets out the truth itself about the gods in its essence, clearly ranks with the highest teachers of the mysteries. These do not think it right to show the divine orders and their characters to their followers through veils; moved by the gods themselves, they announce their powers and their numbers. But to hand down divine things by way of knowledge is the great privilege of the Platonic philosophy. For Plato alone, it seems to me, of all those known to us, has tried to divide and set out methodically the ordered procession of the divine kinds, their differences from one another, the characters common to whole orders, and the characters given to each."

Since Plato uses myths, let us first ask why the ancients made myths, and second how the myths of philosophers differ from those of poets. To answer the first question: the ancients used myths with an eye to two things, the nature of things and our soul. Looking to nature and the making of things, they used myths like this. We come to believe in hidden things from visible things, and in bodiless natures from bodies. Seeing the orderly arrangement of bodies, we understand that some bodiless power governs them; so the heavenly bodies have a power that moves them. And seeing that our body moves, but no longer moves after death, we conclude that some bodiless power moved it. So, seeing that we come to believe in bodiless and hidden things from visible and bodily ones, people adopted myths, so that we might come from visible things to certain hidden natures. For example, when we hear of the gods' adulteries, chains and tearings apart, of the castration of Ouranos and the like, we are not to rest content with the surface meaning, but are to go on to what is hidden and look for the true meaning. In this way, then, looking to the nature of things, myths were used.

Looking to our souls, myths arose like this. As children we live by imagination, and the imagination deals with figures, pictures and things of that kind. So we use myths to keep the imagination in us alive, since that part of us delights in myths. We may also say that a myth is simply a false story that pictures the truth, for a myth is an image of truth. And the soul is an image of the natures above her, so the soul naturally delights in myths, as an image in an image. Since we are brought up on myths from childhood, they must be brought in. So much for the first question, about where myths come from.

Next, let us consider how the myths of philosophers differ from those of poets. Each has something more than the other and something less. The poet's myth has this advantage: it does not let us rest content with the surface meaning, but sends us on to the hidden truth. Who with any intellect would believe that Zeus wanted to lie with Hera on the ground, without waiting to go to the bedroom? So the poet's myth has the advantage of saying things that do not let us stop at the surface, but lead us to search out the hidden truth. Its weakness is that it misleads the young. So Plato sets aside this kind of myth, and sends Homer out of his Republic, because the young, hearing such myths, cannot tell what is allegory and what is not.

The myths of philosophers, on the other hand, do no harm to those who go no further than the surface meaning. For example, they say there are punishments and rivers under the earth, and if we keep to the literal meaning of this we come to no harm. Their weakness is that, because the surface meaning does no harm, we are often content with it and do not search out the hidden truth. We may also say that philosophers' myths have in view the activities of the soul. If we were wholly intellect, with no connection with imagination, we would not need myths, since we would always be in the company of the things of intellect. If, again, we were wholly non-rational, living by imagination and having no other activity, our whole life would have to be myth. But since we have intellect, opinion and imagination, proofs are given for the intellect. So Plato says that if you want to act by intellect, you will have proofs "bound with chains of iron and adamant"; if by opinion, you will have the witness of famous men; and if by imagination, you have myths to stir it. So you will gain something from all of these.

flags.taylor: and hence Plato says
flags.why: Taylor is following Olympiodorus' commentary on the Gorgias here; Plato says no such thing in these words, though "bound with chains of iron and adamant" is from Gorgias 509a.

paragraphs.modern: So Plato rejects the more tragic way of telling myths used by the old poets. They wanted to set up a secret theology about the gods, and so they invented the gods' wanderings, castrations, wars and tearings apart, and many other such symbols of the truth about divine natures that this theology hides. This way he rejects, and says it is utterly unsuited to education. But he thinks those stories about the gods more persuasive and nearer the truth which say that the divine is the cause of all good and of no evil, that it does not change at all, and that it holds in itself the source of truth and never causes anyone else to be deceived. Socrates gives these patterns of theology in the Republic.

So all Plato's myths keep the truth hidden, yet even their outward dress does not clash with our untaught, undistorted first ideas of the divine. They carry with them an image of the ordered world, in which the visible beauty is worthy of the divine, and a beauty more divine than this is set in the hidden lives and powers of its causes.

Next, so that the reader may see where Plato's theological teachings come from, and from which dialogues above all they can be gathered, I give the following translation of what Proclus has written so well on this subject.

"The truth about the gods runs, I may say, through all of Plato's dialogues. In all of them are sown ideas of the first philosophy, reverent, clear and above nature; in some more darkly, in others more plainly. These ideas stir those who can share in them at all towards the immaterial and separate being of the gods. In each part of the universe, and in nature itself, the Craftsman of all that the world contains set likenesses of the unknown being of the gods, so that all things might turn back to the divine through their kinship with it. In the same way, I think, the divine intellect of Plato weaves ideas about the gods into all his writings, and leaves nothing without mention of the divine, so that from all of them a recollection of the whole may be gained and given to true lovers of divine things.
"But if I must set before the reader, out of many, the dialogues that most of all reveal to us the hidden teaching about the gods, I would not be wrong to count among them the Phaedo and the Phaedrus, the Symposium and the Philebus, and with these the Sophist and the Statesman, the Cratylus and the Timaeus. All of these are full, I may say, through and through, of Plato's divine knowledge. In second place after these I would put the myth in the Gorgias and the myth in the Protagoras; also what the Laws says about the gods' providence, and what the tenth book of the Republic says about the Fates, or the mother of the Fates, and the revolutions of the universe. In third place you may put, if you like, those Letters through which we can reach knowledge of divine natures. In these the three kings are mentioned, and very many other divine teachings worthy of Plato's thought are given. So we must look to these and search out in them each order of the gods.
"From the Philebus, then, we may take the knowledge of the one Good, and of the two first principles of things, limit and the unlimited, together with the triad that comes into light from them. You will find all these set out clearly by Plato in that dialogue. From the Timaeus you may get the account of intelligibles, a divine story about the Craftsman as monad, and the fullest truth about the gods of the world. From the Phaedrus you may learn all the kinds of intelligible gods and gods of intellect, and the orders of the gods who are free of the world, set just above the heavenly revolutions. From the Statesman you may get the account of the making in the heavens, of the cycles of the universe, and of the causes in intellect of those cycles. From the Sophist you may learn about all coming-to-be below the moon, and the character of the gods who have the region below the moon as their lot and rule over its births and deaths. And about each of the gods we may get many holy ideas from the Symposium, many from the Cratylus and many from the Phaedo. For in each of these dialogues divine names are mentioned, more or less, and from them those trained in divine things can easily work out by reasoning the character of each.
"We must show, however, that each teaching agrees with Plato's principles and with the hidden traditions of the theologians. For all Greek theology is the offspring of the hidden teaching of Orpheus. Pythagoras first learned the rites of the gods from Aglaophamus, and Plato second received a complete knowledge of the gods from the Pythagorean and Orphic writings. In the Philebus, where he credits the Pythagoreans with the account of the two kinds of principle, limit and the unlimited, he calls them men who live with the gods and are truly blessed. Philolaus the Pythagorean left many fine ideas in writing about these principles, praising how they come forth together into beings and how they make things separately. Again, in the Timaeus, when he tries to teach us about the gods below the moon and their order, Plato turns to the theologians, calls them sons of the gods, and makes them the fathers of the truth about those gods. And finally he gives the orders of the gods below the moon as coming out from the whole, following the procession of the kings of intellect that the theologians handed down. Further, in the Cratylus he follows the theologians' traditions about the order of the divine processions. In the Gorgias he takes up Homer's teaching about the three makers. In short, everywhere he speaks of the gods in line with the theologians' principles, rejecting the tragic side of myth-making, but laying down first assumptions in common with the authors of myths.
"Perhaps someone will object that we are not presenting Plato's theology, scattered everywhere, in a proper way. We are trying, they will say, to pile together different points from different dialogues, as if we wanted to gather many things into one mixture, instead of drawing them all from one and the same source. If that were our aim, we could indeed assign different teachings to different works of Plato, but we would have no leading teaching about the gods. Nor would there be any dialogue that gives us a complete and whole procession of the divine kinds and their ordering with one another. We would be like people who try to make a whole out of parts, because they have no whole before the parts, and who weave the perfect together out of imperfect things, when on the contrary the imperfect should have the first cause of its coming-to-be in the perfect. The Timaeus, for example, will teach us about the intelligible kinds, and the Phaedrus seems to give an ordered account of the first orders of intellect. But where will be the ordering of the things of intellect with the intelligibles? How do the second come from the first? In short, how the divine orders come forth from the one principle of all things, and how, in the birth of the gods, the orders between the One and the complete number are filled in, we will not be able to show.
"Further, it may be said, where is the dignity of your boasted knowledge of divine natures? It is absurd to call 'Platonic' these teachings gathered from many places, which, as you admit, are brought into Plato's philosophy from names foreign to it. And you cannot show the whole truth about divine natures. Perhaps they will add that certain people younger than Plato have handed down in their writings, and left to their pupils, one complete form of philosophy. You, they will say, can produce one whole account of nature from the Timaeus, and from the Republic or the Laws the finest teachings on conduct, which make up one form of philosophy. Only you neglect the work of Plato that holds all the good of the first philosophy and may be called the summit of the whole account, and so you will lack the most perfect knowledge of beings; unless you are so foolish as to boast of mythical fictions, though an analysis of such things has much that is probable but nothing that is proved. Besides, such things are given in the dialogues only by the way. The myth in the Protagoras is put in for the sake of political knowledge and the proofs about it. In the same way, the myth in the Republic is put in for the sake of justice, and the one in the Gorgias for the sake of self-control. For Plato joins mythical stories to inquiries about conduct, not for the sake of the myths, but for the sake of the main aim: so that we may not only train the intellect-part of the soul through arguments for and against, but also that the divine part of the soul may more fully receive the knowledge of beings, through its sympathy with more hidden things. From other kinds of discourse we are like people forced to accept the truth; but from myths we are moved in an inexpressible way, and call up our undistorted ideas, honouring the hidden teaching they contain.
"So, it seems to me, Timaeus rightly thinks we should set out the divine kinds by following the inventors of myths as sons of the gods, and accept that they always produce second natures from first ones, even though they speak without proof. For this kind of discourse is not proof, but inspired, the offspring of divine inspiration. The ancients invented it not from necessity but to persuade, aiming not at bare instruction but at sympathy with the things themselves. And if you want to study the causes not only of myths but of other theological teachings, you will find that some are scattered in the dialogues for the sake of ethics, and others for the sake of the study of nature. In the Philebus Plato discusses limit and the unlimited for the sake of pleasure and of the life of intellect, since I think the latter are kinds of the former. In the Timaeus the account of the intelligible gods is taken up for the sake of the study of nature that is proposed. That is why images must everywhere be known from their patterns: the patterns of material things must be immaterial, of perceptible things intelligible, and of natural forms separate from nature. In the Phaedrus Plato praises the place above the heavens, the depth below the heavens and every kind below that, for the sake of the madness of love: how souls recollect, and how they pass from here to there. Everywhere, then, the main aim, so to speak, is either about nature or about the city, and the ideas about divine natures are brought in either for discovery or for completion. How, then, can a theory like yours still be reverent and above nature, and worth studying above all else, when it cannot show the whole in itself, or the perfect, or what leads in Plato's writings, but lacks all these, is forced and not natural, and has not a true order but one added from outside, as in a play? These are the points that may be urged against our plan.
"To this objection I will give a fair and clear reply. I say that Plato everywhere speaks of the gods in line with ancient opinions and the nature of things. Sometimes, for the sake of explaining the matter in hand, he takes it back to the principles of the teachings, and from there, as from a high lookout, he views the nature of the thing in question. But sometimes he makes theological knowledge the main aim. In the Phaedrus his subject is intelligible beauty and the sharing in beauty that passes from there through all things; and in the Symposium it is the order of love.
"But if we must find, in one dialogue of Plato, the complete account, whole and connected, reaching to the full number of theology, I will perhaps state a paradox, which only our own circle will see. Yet we must be bold, since we have begun, and affirm against our opponents that the Parmenides, and the hidden ideas of this dialogue, will give you all you want. In this dialogue all the divine kinds come forth in order from the first cause and show how they hang from one another. The highest, akin to the One and first in nature, have a way of existing marked by unity, hidden and simple. The last are multiplied, divided into many parts, and greater in number, but lower in power than those of a higher order. And those in the middle, in fitting proportion, are more compound than their causes but simpler than their own offspring. In short, all the axioms of theological knowledge appear complete in this dialogue, and all the divine orders are shown existing in connection. So this is nothing else than the famous birth of the gods, and the coming forth of every kind of being from the inexpressible and unknown cause of all. So the Parmenides kindles in the lovers of Plato the whole, full light of theological knowledge. After it, the dialogues mentioned above give out parts of the hidden teaching about the gods. All of them, I may say, share in divine wisdom and stir our natural ideas of the divine. We must refer all the parts of this hidden teaching to these dialogues, and these again to the one complete account of the Parmenides. In this way, I think, we will hang the less perfect from the perfect, and parts from wholes, and will show accounts that are like the things they explain, as Plato's Timaeus says accounts should be. This is our answer to the objection that may be raised against us. So we refer Plato's theology to the Parmenides, just as everyone with the least intelligence agrees that the Timaeus holds the whole knowledge of nature."

flags.taylor: For all the Grecian theology is the progeny of the mystic doctrine of Orpheus
flags.why: This is Proclus' view of the history of Greek religion, which modern historians do not share; the story of Pythagoras and Aglaophamus comes from Iamblichus.

flags.taylor: the Parmenides, and the mystic conceptions of this dialogue, will accomplish all you desire
flags.why: That the Parmenides is a theology of the gods is the reading of Iamblichus, Syrianus and Proclus. Many readers, ancient and modern, take it as a logical exercise.

paragraphs.modern: A reader who understands the outline we have given here of Plato's theology, and who has also fully mastered the hidden meaning of the Parmenides, will at once accept all that Proclus says here. I trust that meaning is set out well enough, with Proclus' help, in the introduction and notes to that dialogue.

The next important teaching of Plato, in order, is the teaching on Forms. So much is said about them in the notes on the Parmenides that little is left to add here. That little is this. The divine Pythagoras, and all who truly received his teachings, among whom Plato ranks highest, said there are many orders of beings: intelligible, of intellect, of discursive reason, natural, or in short living and bodily beings. The coming-forth of things, the lowering that naturally goes with it, and the power of difference within kinds of the same rank, give being to the whole multitude of bodily and bodiless natures. So they said there are three orders in the whole range of beings: the intelligible, that of discursive reason, and the perceptible. In each of these, Forms exist, marked by the special character of the natures that hold them. The intelligible Forms they placed among divine natures, together with the making, pattern and final causes of things, in their order. If these three causes sometimes come together and are united (as Aristotle says they are), this surely does not happen in the lowest works of nature, but in the first and best causes of all things. Because of their overflowing fruitfulness, these have the power to produce all things; and because they turn the natures they produce towards themselves and make them like themselves, they are the patterns of all things. And since these divine causes act for their own sake and because of their own goodness, do they not show the final cause too? Since intelligible Forms are like this, and lead so much good to the whole, they complete the divine orders, though they exist above all in the intelligible order held in the Craftsman of the universe. The Forms of discursive reason imitate the Forms of intellect, which exist before them. They make the order of soul like the order of intellect, and hold all things at a second level.

flags.taylor: But dianoëtic forms or ideas imitate the intellectual
flags.why: Taylor's text runs together intelligible, intellectual and "dianoetic" Forms, following Syrianus; the three ranks are the later Platonists' and are not set out in Plato.

paragraphs.modern: These Forms, seen in divine natures, have the power to make. In us they only know, and no longer make, because our wings have fallen away, that is, our powers of intellect have been lowered. As Plato says in the Phaedrus, when the soul's winged powers are perfect and feathered for flight, she lives on high and governs the world together with divine natures. In the Timaeus he clearly says that the Craftsman planted these Forms of discursive reason in souls, in geometric, arithmetic and harmonic proportions. In the Republic (in the divided line of the sixth book) he calls them images of intelligibles, and so for the most part he does not hesitate to call them "of intellect," since they are the patterns of perceptible natures. In the Phaedo he says that they cause our recollection, because learning is nothing but recollection of these middle Forms of discursive reason. From them the productive powers of nature draw, and, inspired by them, give birth to all the things that appear in the world.

Plato did not think that things which can be defined (what we now call abstract ideas) are the only universals. Before these he placed the principles that produce knowledge, which live in the soul by its very being, as the Phaedrus and Phaedo show. In the tenth book of the Republic he honours the separate Forms that exist in a divine intellect. In the Phaedrus he says that souls raised to the place above the heavens see Justice itself, Self-control itself and Knowledge itself. And in the Phaedo he proves the immortality of the soul from the assumption that there are separate Forms.

Syrianus, in his commentary on the thirteenth book of Aristotle's Metaphysics, defends Socrates, Plato, the followers of Parmenides and the Pythagoreans. He shows that these divine men did not bring in Forms in the ordinary sense of words, as Chrysippus, Archedemus and many of the later Stoics thought, for Forms differ in many ways from things named by custom. Nor, he says, do they exist together with intellect in the way that those thin ideas we call universals, drawn from perceptible things, do, as Longinus supposed; for what has no substance cannot exist together with intellect. Nor are Forms, for these men, concepts, as Cleanthes later said. Nor is a Form a defining account, nor a form in matter; for these exist in putting together and taking apart, and lean towards matter. But Forms are perfect, simple, immaterial and partless natures. And what wonder is it, says Syrianus, if we separate things so far apart? We do not follow Plutarch, Atticus and Democritus here either. Because general accounts always exist in the being of the soul, they thought these accounts were the Forms. They do separate them from the universal in perceptible things; yet we should not join into one and the same thing the accounts of the soul, and an intellect like ours, with the pattern Forms that are immaterial and with the Craftsman's acts of thought. As the divine Plato says, it is the work of our soul to gather things into one by reasoning, and to recollect those high sights we once saw when we governed the universe together with God. Boethus the Peripatetic, with whom we should put Cornutus, thought that Forms are the same as universals in perceptible things. But if these universals come before particular things, they do not come before them in such a way as to be free of their relation to them, nor do they exist as the causes of particular things, and both these belong to Forms. Or if they come after particular things, as many like to say, how can things that come later, which have no being of their own but are only thin ideas, have the dignity of the Forms that make things?

flags.taylor: Plutarch, Atticus, and Democritus
flags.why: The "Democritus" here is a Platonist of the third century AD, not the atomist; Taylor does not say so.

paragraphs.modern: How, then, says Syrianus, do Forms exist, according to those who love to contemplate the truth? We answer: in the manner of intelligibles and in fours (noētōs kai tetradikōs) in the Living Being itself, the lowest point of the intelligible order; but in the manner of intellect and in tens (noerōs kai dekadikōs) in the intellect of the Craftsman of the universe. For, according to the Pythagorean hymn,

"Divine number goes forth from the hidden depths of the undying monad until it reaches the divine tetrad, which brought forth the mother of all things, the receiver of all, revered, setting a limit round all things, unmoved and untiring, which both the immortal gods and men born of earth call the sacred decad."

(Taylor gives the Greek of the Pythagorean hymn translated just above: "Divine number goes forth, as the Pythagorean hymn to it says, from the hidden depths of the undying monad until it reaches the divine tetrad, which brought forth the mother of all, the receiver of all, revered, setting a limit round all things, unturning and untiring; the immortal gods and earth-born men call her the sacred decad.")
