paragraphs.modern: This is how the Forms exist, according to Orpheus, Pythagoras and Plato. Or, to put it more plainly: an intellect that is sufficient to itself, and is the most perfect cause, rules over the wholes of the universe and through them governs all its parts. While it makes all the natures of the world and does them good by its providence, it keeps its own most divine and spotless purity. It lights up all things, but it is not mixed with the things it lights up. This intellect holds in the depths of its being a world of Forms, full of every kind of form, and so it shuts out from its activity both lack of a cause and chance. Because it gives every good and all possible beauty to what it makes, it turns the universe towards itself and makes it like its own all-formed nature. Its activity is like its thinking, and it thinks all things, since it is most perfect. So there is nothing among true beings that is not held in the being of intellect. It always sets up in itself Forms that are not different from itself and its being, but complete it, and give to the whole of things a cause that is at once productive, a pattern, and an end. For it acts as intellect; the Forms it holds are patterns, since they are forms; and they act from themselves, out of their own overflowing goodness. These are Plato's teachings on the Forms. Clever arguments and ignorance may oppose them, but they will never refute them.

From this intelligible world, full of Forms of every kind, the perceptible world, according to Plato, flows out for ever. It depends on its maker, intellect, as a shadow depends on the body that casts it. Its maker is a god of intellect, and both the being and the activity of intellect are set in eternity. So the perceptible universe, which is the effect or product of such an activity, must exist together with its cause; in other words, it must flow out from it for ever. This will be clear if we consider that whatever comes to be comes to be by art, by nature, or by power. Whatever works by nature or by art must come before what it produces. But whatever works by power has its products existing together with it, as the sun produces light that exists with it, fire heat, and snow cold. If the maker of the universe had made it by art, he would not make it simply be, but be in some particular way, for all art produces form. Then where would the world get its being from? If he made it by nature, then, since what makes by nature gives something of itself to what it makes, and the maker of the world is bodiless, the world, the product of such an activity, would have to be bodiless. It remains, then, that the Craftsman made the universe by power alone. But whatever is produced by power exists together with the cause that holds this power. So things produced in this way cannot be destroyed unless the producing cause loses its power. So the divine intellect that produced the perceptible universe made it exist together with himself.

flags.taylor: must be consubsistent with its cause, or, in other words, must be a perpetual emanation from it
flags.why: Whether Plato's Timaeus means that the world had no beginning in time was disputed in antiquity. Proclus and the later Platonists said it had none; Aristotle, Plutarch and Atticus read Plato as saying it had one.

paragraphs.modern: This world, depending on its divine maker, who is himself an intelligible world full of the original Forms of all things, is always flowing when we look at its bodily nature. It is always on the way to being (en tōi gignesthai), and compared with its pattern it has no stability or reality of being. But when we see it as alive with a divine soul, receiving the light of all the gods above the world, and itself the home of the gods on whom bodies depend, Plato in the Timaeus calls it a blessed god. The great body of this world, which exists always spread out in time, may properly be called a whole that exists as a whole, because it lasts for ever, though this is only a flowing eternity. So Plato calls it a whole of wholes. By the other wholes it contains he means the heavenly spheres, the sphere of fire, the whole of the air taken as one great sphere, the whole earth and the whole sea. These spheres, which Platonic writers call "parts that exist as wholes," Plato takes to be everlasting as wholes. If the body of the world is everlasting, so must its larger parts be, because they are so closely related to it, and so that the wholes that exist as parts, such as all individual things, may stand in the last rank of things.

Plato calls the world, taken as one great all-embracing whole, a divine living being. In the same way every whole it contains is a world. It has, first, a unity complete in itself, coming from the inexpressible, by which it is a god; second, a divine intellect; third, a divine soul; and last, a body made divine. So each of these wholes is the producing cause of all the multitude it contains, and for this reason it is called a whole before its parts. It has an eternal form that holds all its parts together and makes the whole last for ever, so it does not need those parts to complete its being. That these wholes, which rank so high in the universe, are alive follows with the certainty of geometry. For, as Theophrastus rightly says, wholes would have less authority than parts, and eternal things than perishable ones, if they had no soul.

We have climbed on bold but humble wings to the inexpressible principle of things, and, standing with every eye shut at the entrance of the inner shrine, found that we could say nothing about him, but only show our doubts and our failure. From there we came down to his hidden and most revered offspring, passed through the bright world of the Forms holding fast to the golden chain of the divine, and ended our downward flight in the material universe and its undying wholes. Let us stop for a while, then, and look at the height and grandeur of the view this journey sets before us. We see the vast empire of the divine. At the top its limit is a principle so inexpressible that all language breaks down about it; at the bottom, the vast body of the world. Directly after this vast unknown we see a mighty, all-embracing One. Because it is next to what is in every way beyond grasp, it has much of the inexpressible and unknown. From this principle of principles, in which all things exist as in their cause, drowned in light beyond being and wrapped in depths no one can sound, we see a beautiful family of principles. All share richly in the inexpressible, all bear the hidden marks of the divine, all have an overflowing fullness of good. From these dazzling summits, these inexpressible flowers, these divine offspring, we next see being, life, intellect, soul, nature and body hanging down: monads hanging from henads, natures made divine coming out from gods. Each of these monads also leads a series that stretches from it down to the last of things, and that, while it comes forth from its leader, also remains in it and returns to it. All these principles and all their offspring are in the end centred and rooted, by their summits, in the first great all-embracing One. So all beings come from the first being and are held in it; all intellects flow from one first intellect; all souls from one first soul; all natures flower from one first nature; and all bodies come from the living and shining body of the world. Lastly, all these great monads are held in the first One, from which both they and all the series that hang from them are unfolded into light. So this first One is truly the henad of henads, the monad of monads, the principle of principles, the God of gods, one and all things, and yet one before all.

Such, according to Plato, are the flights of the true philosopher, and such the great and splendid view he sees. Only by climbing these bright heights do the soul's natural longings for the divine find something worthy of their desire. Only here does inquiry finally rest, doubt die in certainty, and knowledge lose itself in the inexpressible.

Here, perhaps, some solemn objector will speak up, a narrow mind that is sharp but sees nothing clearly and soundly. He will say that all this is very grand, but that it flies too high for human beings; that it is only spiritual pride; that no truths in morals or theology matter unless they suit the level of the weakest mind; and that all a person needs to know about God or himself is so plain that "he who runs may read." To such cant, for it is nothing more, cant born of the deepest ignorance and often joined with the saddest envy, I answer with questions. Is the Delphic command, KNOW YOURSELF, a small thing? Can every person do it? Can anyone truly know himself without knowing his rank in the scale of being? Can he do that without knowing which natures he stands above and which stand above him? And can he know that without knowing as much about those natures as he can? Will the objector dare to say that every person is equal to this hard task? That a man who rushes from the forge or the mines, his soul twisted, crushed and bruised by low manual trades, and wildly presumes to teach theology to a deceived audience, has mastered this high and most important knowledge? For my part, the only truths I know that are so plain and open to everyone are axioms: those self-evident first principles of knowledge that shine by their own light, that are the soul's natural, undistorted ideas, and to which anyone who will not agree deserves, as Aristotle rightly says, either pity or correction. In short, if the test of all knowledge in morals and theology is that it must be plain at once to everyone, seen at a careless glance, why do we need schools? Education is absurd, and the labour of inquiry is wasted. Let us shut Wisdom up at once in the dungeons of Folly, call Ignorance back from her wild wastes, and bar the gates of Knowledge for ever.

flags.taylor: he who rushes from the forge, or the mines, with a soul distorted, crushed and bruised by base mechanical arts
flags.why: This is Taylor's attack on the working-class lay preachers of his own day; it is his opinion, not Plato's, and it is kept here only because the modern version leaves nothing out.

paragraphs.modern: We have now taken a general view of the great world, and come down from the intelligible universe to the perceptible one. Still holding to the golden chain that is bound round the top of Olympus, and from which all things hang, let us come down to the small world, the human being. For a human being holds in himself, in part, everything that the world holds divinely and as a whole. So, according to Plato, he has an intellect that is always active, and a rational soul that comes from the same father and life-giving goddess who are the causes of the intellect and soul of the universe. He also has a vehicle of ether, like the heavens, and an earthly body made of the four elements, to which it also corresponds.

flags.taylor: he is endued with an intellect subsisting in energy
flags.why: Taylor here speaks of an intellect in us that is "always active"; in the next paragraph he follows the later Platonists, who said that our intellect is not always active and needs a higher intellect to perfect it.

paragraphs.modern: As for his rational part, in which the being of a human consists, we have already shown that it moves itself, and that it stands between intellect, which does not move in being or in activity, and nature, which both moves and is moved. Because of this middle place, Plato says in the Timaeus that the soul of the world, from which all particular souls come, is a middle between what is indivisible and what is divided among bodies. That is, the world-soul is a middle between the intellect of the world and the whole bodily life the world shares in. In the same way the human soul is a middle between a daemonic intellect, set just above our being, which also raises and perfects it, and the bodily life spread through our body, which causes its birth, feeding and growth. In the Phaedrus Plato calls this daemonic intellect the one that contemplates, and the pilot of the soul. So the highest part of the human soul is the summit of discursive reason (to akrotaton tēs dianoias), the power that reasons with knowledge, and this summit is our intellect. But since our very being is marked by reason, this summit of ours is rational. Though it is active, its union with things themselves is slackened. Though it acts from itself and holds intelligibles in its being, its kinship with the step-by-step nature of soul, and its leaning towards the divided, make it fall short of the perfection of a being and activity of intellect that is deeply undivided and united. And the intelligibles it holds fall short of the supremely bright, self-shining nature of the first intelligibles. So, to gain a wholly undivided knowledge, it needs to be perfected by an intellect whose activity is always awake and never slackens; and its intelligibles, to become perfect, need the light that comes from separate intelligibles. So Aristotle rightly compares the intelligibles of our intellect to colours, which need the brightness of the sun. He calls an intellect of this kind intellect in potential, both because it ranks below an intellect that is intellect in its very being, and because it receives the full perfection of its nature from a separate intellect. The middle part of the rational soul Plato calls dianoia, discursive reason: the power that, as we have said, reasons with knowledge, taking the starting points of its reasoning, the axioms, from intellect. And the lowest part of the rational soul is opinion, which in the Sophist he defines as the power that knows the conclusion of discursive reason. This power also knows the universal in perceptible particulars, for example that every human being has two feet. But it knows only the hoti, that a thing is so, and not the dioti, why it is so; knowing why belongs to discursive reason.

flags.taylor: which in his Sophista he defines to be that power which knows the conclusion of dianoia
flags.why: Sophist 264a defines opinion as the completion of thinking (dianoia), "when the soul silently affirms or denies"; "knows the conclusion" is the later Platonists' reading.

paragraphs.modern: This is Plato's division of the rational part of our nature, which he rightly takes to be the true human being, since the being of anything lies in its best part.

After this comes the non-rational nature. Its summit is imagination, the power that perceives everything with shape and size, and so it may be called a thinking in shapes (morphōtikē noēsis). This power, as Iamblichus finely says, grows over, as it were, and shapes all the powers of the soul. It stirs up in opinion the lights that come from the senses, and fixes in the life that is spread out with the body the impressions that come down from intellect. So, says Proclus, it wraps itself round the undividedness of true intellect, takes the shape of all formless kinds, and becomes wholly everything from which discursive reason and our undivided reason are made. So too it is passively all the things that intellect is without being acted on, and that is why Aristotle calls it passive intellect. Below it are anger and desire: anger like a raging lion, desire like a many-headed beast. The whole is bounded by sensation, which is only a passive perception of things. So Plato rightly says it is more a being-affected than a knowing, since the first is marked by inertness and the second by activity.

Further, so that the soul may be joined fittingly to this coarse earthly body, Plato says two vehicles are needed between them: one of ether and one of air. The ethereal vehicle is simple and immaterial, while this dense earthly body is compound and material.

flags.taylor: two vehicles, according to Plato, are necessary as media
flags.why: The teaching of the soul's "vehicles" belongs to the later Platonists (Proclus, Hermias); Plato only hints at it, for example in the soul's "vehicle" at Timaeus 41e.

paragraphs.modern: So the soul stands between undivided natures and natures divided among bodies. It produces and builds the second, and sets up within itself the higher causes it comes from. So it holds beforehand, as their pattern, the natures it comes before as their cause; and it has by sharing, as the flowers of the first natures, the causes of its own being. So it holds in its being immaterial forms of material things, bodiless forms of bodily things, and unextended forms of things marked by extension. But it holds intelligibles as an image: it receives their undivided forms in a divided way, the single in a varied way, and the unmoving in a self-moving way. So soul is all things. Olympiodorus finely calls it a statue of all forms (pammorphon agalma), for it holds the things above it by sharing, and the things below it as their pattern.

The soul is always moving, and this "always" is not eternal but in time. For what is truly eternal, as intellect is, is wholly still and has no activities that pass from one thing to another. So the soul's motions must go in cycles. Motion is a change from some things into others, and beings are limited in number and size. Since they are limited, there cannot be endless change in a straight line, nor can what is always moving come to a finish. So what is always moving will go from the same to the same, and so move in a cycle. So too the human soul, and every soul in the world, has cycles and returns of its own life. Because it is measured by time, it acts step by step and has a motion of its own. But everything that moves for ever and shares in time goes round in cycles and goes from the same to the same. So the soul, since it has motion and acts in time, will have cycles of motion and returns to its first state.

According to Plato, the human soul is one of those souls that follow the gods of the world only some of the time, since it ranks just after the daemons and heroes, who attend the gods for ever. So it has the power to come down without end into becoming, the region below the moon, and to go back up from becoming to real being. Since it does not live with the divine for an endless time, neither will it be busy with bodies for all the time after. For, according to both Plato and Aristotle, what has no beginning in time cannot have an end, and what has no end must have no beginning. It remains, then, that every soul goes through cycles of rising out of becoming and coming down into becoming, and that this will never stop, through endless time.

flags.taylor: hence it possesses a power of descending infinitely into generation
flags.why: That every human soul comes down and goes up again for ever is the teaching of Proclus; Iamblichus and Plotinus held different views, and Plato's own words (Phaedrus 248e-249a) speak of cycles of ten thousand years.

paragraphs.modern: From all this it follows that the soul, while it lives on earth, is in a fallen state, a deserter from the divine, an exile from the world of light. So in the seventh book of the Republic Plato, looking at our life with regard to education and the lack of it, compares us to people in a cave under the earth. They have been kept there since childhood, chained so that they can look only straight ahead, towards the back of the cave, while the entrance behind them opens to the light; and the chains stop them from turning round. He imagines, too, a fire burning far above and behind them, and between the fire and the prisoners a road higher up, along which a low wall has been built. Along this wall men carry all kinds of objects, and statues of people and other animals in wood and stone. Some of these men are talking and some are silent. As for the prisoners in this cave, they see nothing of themselves or of each other, or of what is carried past, except the shadows that the fire throws on the wall in front of them. He imagines, too, that the wall of the prison in front of them gives back an echo, so that when the prisoners hear anyone speak they think it is only the passing shadow.

flags.taylor: but the shadows formed by the fire falling on the opposite part of the cave
flags.why: Taylor's summary moves the entrance: in Plato (Republic 514a-515b) the prisoners face the back wall, and the entrance and the fire are behind them. The modern version follows Plato.

paragraphs.modern: First, as we noted in the notes on that book, the road higher up, between the fire and the prisoners, shows that there is a climb within the cave itself, from a lower to a higher life. By this climb Plato means the study of the objects of discursive reason in mathematics. The shadows in the cave correspond to the shadows of visible things, and visible things are the direct images of the Forms of discursive reason, the ideas the soul shares in by its very being. So the objects whose shadows these are must correspond to the objects of discursive reason. So discursive reason, training itself on these, must draw out their principles from their hiding places, and see them not in images but as existing in itself, folded together without division.
Next he says:

"the man who is to be led out of the cave will more easily see what is in the heavens, and the heavens themselves, by looking at night at the light of the stars and the moon, than by looking by day at the sun and the sunlight."

By this he means the contemplation of intelligibles. The stars and their light imitate the intelligibles, so far as they all share in the form of the sun, just as the intelligibles are all marked by the nature of the Good.

After seeing these, when the eye has grown used to the light through them, he must see the sun itself last, in the visible region. In the same way, according to Plato, the Form of the Good must be seen last in the intelligible region. He adds, divinely, that it is hardly to be seen; for we can be joined to it only through the intelligible, at whose doorway the rising soul sees it.

In short, according to Plato, the soul can be restored on earth to the likeness of God that she left when she came down, and can rise again after death to the intelligible world, only by practising the purifying virtues and the contemplative virtues. The first clean her of the stains of a mortal nature, and the second raise her to the sight of true being. For in this way, as Plato says in the Timaeus,
"the soul, becoming sound and whole, will reach the form of her first condition."

The purifying virtues must come before the contemplative ones, since no one can look at truth while shaken by the turmoil of the passions. The rational soul stands between intellect and the non-rational nature. She can be with the intellect above her, without being torn apart, only when she has become free of sharing the feelings of the lower natures. So by the purifying virtues we become sound, freed from the passions as from diseases; and we become whole by taking back intellect and knowledge as our own proper parts, which happens through contemplating the truth. Plato also clearly teaches that our desertion of better natures can be healed only by fleeing from here, when in the Theaetetus he defines philosophy as a flight from earthly evils. This shows that passions are born only with mortal things. In the same dialogue he also says that
"evils can never be done away with, nor can they have their place among the gods; they must go round this earthly home and mortal nature."

Those who are subject to coming-to-be and passing away can also be affected against their nature, and this is the beginning of evils. In the same dialogue he adds how our flight from evil is to be made.
"We must flee from here to there," he says, "and the flight is becoming like God, as far as a human being can; and becoming like him is becoming just and holy, with practical wisdom."

flags.taylor: in conjunction with intellectual prudence
flags.why: Theaetetus 176b has "with wisdom" (meta phronēseōs); Taylor's "intellectual" is his own addition.

paragraphs.modern: Whoever wants to escape evils must first turn away from mortal nature, since those mixed with it cannot avoid being filled with the evils that come with it. We fell into this mortal home, and so were linked with evils, by fleeing from the divine and losing the wings that lift us up. In the same way, by giving up our sharing in mortal feeling, and by growing the virtues like wings, we return to the home of pure and true good and to the possession of divine happiness. The being of a human stands in the middle, between the daemons, who always know the divine by intellect, and those beings who by nature can never understand him. It rises to the first and sinks to the second by having intellect or giving it up. Because of its two-sided nature, it becomes at home both with the likeness of God and with the likeness of beasts.

So when the soul has won back her first perfection, as far as she can while living on earth, by practising the purifying and contemplative virtues, she returns after death, as Plato says in the Timaeus, to the star she belongs to, from which she fell, and lives a blessed life. Then too, as he says in the Phaedrus, having her wings again, she governs the world together with the gods. This is the finest end of her labours. This is what he calls in the Phaedo "a great contest and a great hope." This is the most perfect fruit of philosophy: to make her at home again with what is truly beautiful and lead her back to it, to free her from this earthly home as from an underground cave of material life, to raise her to the brightness of the heavens, and to place her in the Isles of the Blessed.

From this account of the human soul follows that most important teaching of Plato: our soul holds all knowledge in her very being, and whatever knowledge she gains in this life is really only the recovery of what she once had. Plato rightly calls this recovery recollection. Not because we actually remember it in this life, but because the soul really takes back what she lost through her forgetful union with the body. Pointing to this knowledge that is part of the soul's being, which teaching calls out of its sleep, Plato says in the Sophist that "we know all things as in a dream, and again do not know them when we are awake." So too, as Proclus rightly says, it is clear that the soul does not gather her knowledge from perceptible things, nor find the whole and the one from particular, divided things. We should not think that things which have no real being in any way lead the soul to knowledge; that things which oppose each other and are doubtful come before knowledge, which is always the same; that things which change in all sorts of ways produce accounts that are fixed in unity; or that things without limit cause intelligence that has limits. So the truth of eternal things must not be taken from the many, nor the sorting of universals from perceptible things, nor a judgment about what is good from non-rational natures. The soul must go into herself, and search within herself for the true and the good and the eternal accounts of things.

flags.taylor: we know all things as in a dream, and are again ignorant of them, according to vigilant perception
flags.why: Taylor credits this to the Sophist, but the words are from the Statesman (277d).

paragraphs.modern: We have said that teaching wakes up the soul's sleeping knowledge, and Plato thought that mathematics does this best of all. So he says that theoretical arithmetic gives no small help to our climb towards real being, and frees us from the wandering and ignorance that belong to perceptible nature. He thinks geometry too is a great help towards knowing the Good, when it is pursued not for practical uses but as a way of climbing to intelligible being. Astronomy is also useful for searching out the maker of all things and contemplating, as in the brightest images, the world of Forms and its inexpressible cause. And lastly music, studied rightly, helps our climb, that is, when we turn from perceptible harmony to the contemplation of the harmony of Forms, which is divine. But unless we use mathematics in this way, Plato rightly thinks the study of it incomplete, useless and worthless. For, in his philosophy, the true end of a human being is to become like God, as perfectly as human nature can. Whatever helps towards this must be pursued eagerly. Whatever leads elsewhere, however necessary it may be for the needs and comforts of mere animal life, is small and low by comparison. So we must pass quickly from things seen and heard to those seen only by the eye of intellect. For the mathematical sciences, studied rightly, stir the knowledge that is in the soul. They wake its intelligence, purify its discursive reason, call its own Forms out of their sleep, remove the forgetting and ignorance we are born with, and loosen the bonds that come from our union with a non-rational nature. So Plato says finely, in the seventh book of the Republic, that
"through these studies the soul has an organ cleaned and lit up again, which other pursuits blind and bury, an organ more worth saving than ten thousand eyes, since truth is seen by it alone."

Dialectic, which Plato in the Republic calls the coping-stone of the mathematical sciences, is the master study that leads us up to intelligible being above all. I have said much about this first of the sciences in the introduction and notes to the Parmenides. It is quite different from ordinary logic, and is the same as what Aristotle calls first philosophy and wisdom. It is enough to note here how dialectic differs from mathematical knowledge. Mathematics starts from assumptions; dialectic is free of them. Dialectic can know universals; it climbs to the Good, the highest cause of all, and takes the Good as the goal of its climb. Mathematics first sets up definite starting points for itself, and from them shows what follows; so it does not go towards the first principle, but towards the conclusion. So Plato does not throw mathematical knowledge out of the sciences. He says it is next in rank to the one science that is the summit of all. Nor does he blame it for not knowing its own starting points. He sees that it receives them from the master science, dialectic, and that, holding them without proof, it proves from them the propositions that follow.

flags.taylor: the same with what Aristotle calls the first philosophy and wisdom
flags.why: That Plato's dialectic is Aristotle's "first philosophy" is Taylor's view, following the later Platonists; Aristotle himself sets dialectic below first philosophy.

paragraphs.modern: So Socrates in the Republic, speaking of the power of dialectic, says that it surrounds all studies like a protecting wall. It lifts those who use it up to the Good itself and the first henads. It cleans the eye of the soul, settles itself in true beings and in the one principle of all things, and ends at last in what is no longer an assumption. Since the power of dialectic is so great, and the end of this road so mighty, it must never be confused with arguments that deal only with opinion. Dialectic guards the sciences, and the way to it passes through them; but those arguments have no part at all in knowledge that is taught. We may add that reasoning based on opinion looks only at what appears. The dialectical method tries to reach the One itself, always using steps of climbing for this, and at last ends finely in the nature of the Good. So it is very different from mere logic, which governs the imagination that deals in proofs, is of a lower rank, and enjoys only quarrelsome debate. For Plato's dialectic mostly uses division and analysis as its first methods, since they imitate the procession of beings from the One and their return to it again. It also sometimes uses definitions and proofs, and before these the method of defining, and before that the method of dividing. Mere logic, on the other hand, which deals only with opinion, lacks the proofs that cannot be argued against.

Here is a sample of the method of analysis in Plato's dialectic. There are three kinds of analysis. The first is a climb from perceptible things to the first intelligibles. The second is a climb, through things proved and partly proved, to propositions that are not proved but immediate. The third goes from an assumption to principles that are not assumptions. Plato gives a wonderful example of the first kind in Diotima's speech in the Symposium. There he climbs from the beauty of bodies to the beauty of souls; from this to the beauty of right studies; from this again to the beauty of laws; from the beauty of laws to "the great sea of beauty" (to polu pelagos tou kalou); and going on in this way he reaches at last the Beautiful itself.

flags.taylor: to the beauty in laws; from the beauty in laws to the ample sea of beauty
flags.why: Taylor follows Olympiodorus' list; in the Symposium (210a-d) the order is bodies, souls, practices and laws, kinds of knowledge, then the great sea of beauty.

paragraphs.modern: The second kind of analysis is this. We take the thing we are looking into as an assumption. We look at what comes before it, and prove these from what comes after, climbing to what comes before, until we reach the first thing, which we accept. Then, starting from this, we come down step by step to the thing we were looking into. Here is an example from Plato's Phaedrus. The question is whether the soul is immortal. Taking this as an assumption, we next ask whether it is always moving. When this is proved, the next question is whether what is always moving moves itself. When this is proved too, we consider whether what moves itself is the source of motion, and then whether the source has no beginning. Once this is accepted as agreed, and also that what has no beginning cannot perish, the proof of the question is gathered like this. If there is a source, it has no beginning and cannot perish. What moves itself is the source of motion. The soul moves itself. So the soul (that is, the rational soul) cannot perish, has no beginning, and is immortal.

Of the third kind of analysis, which goes from what is assumed to what is not assumed, Plato gives a very beautiful example in the first hypothesis of his Parmenides. Taking as his assumption that the One is, he goes through an ordered series of denials. These denials do not take something away from their subject; they produce things that are, as it were, their opposites. At last he takes away the assumption itself, that the One is. He denies of it every account and every name, and so he plainly denies of it not only that it is, but even denial. For all things come after the One: things known, knowledge, and the tools of knowledge. So, starting from what is assumed, he ends in what is not assumed and truly inexpressible.

Having taken a general view of both the great world and the small world, the human being, I will end this account of Plato's main teachings with an outline of what he says about providence and fate. The subject matters greatly, and that prince of philosophers happily clears away the difficulties that surround it.

First, then, providence, as people commonly understand it, is the cause of good to the things it cares for, and fate is the cause of a certain linking among things that come to be. Granting this, let us consider what the things are that are linked. Of beings, some have their being in eternity and others in time. By beings whose being is in eternity I mean those whose activity, as well as their being, is eternal. By beings that are in time in their very being I mean those whose being is always coming to be, even if this goes on for endless time. Between these two extremes are natures whose being is in some way lasting and better than becoming, or than a flowing existence, but whose activity is measured by time. For every procession from first things to last must go through middle terms. So the middle term between these two extremes must be either what has an eternal being but an activity that needs time, or the reverse, what has a being in time but an eternal activity. But the second cannot exist; if it did, activity would come before being. So the middle term must be what has an eternal being but an activity in time. The three orders that make up this first, middle and last are the order of intellect, the order of soul, and the order of body. From what we have said already about the ranks of beings, it is clear that the order of intellect is set in eternity both in being and in activity; that the order of body is always coming to be, either in endless time or in part of time; and that the order of soul is eternal in being but in time in activity. Where, then, shall we put things that are spread out in places or in times, and yet are ranked together with each other and feel with each other through being linked? Clearly they must be put among the natures that are bodily and moved by another. For of the things above the order of bodies, some are above both place and time, and others, though they act in time, seem quite free of any link with place.

So the things governed and linked by fate are wholly bodily and moved by another. Once this is shown, it is plain that, if fate is a cause of linking, we must say that it rules over natures that are bodily and moved by another. If we look for the nearest cause of bodies, the cause by which things moved by another are moved, breathe and are held together, we find that it is nature, whose work is to produce, to feed and to make grow. This power exists not only in us and all other animals and plants. Much more must there be, before particular bodies, one nature of the world, which holds and moves all bodies. It follows that nature is the cause of linked things, and that it is in nature that we must look for fate. So fate is nature: that bodiless power which is the one life of the world. It rules over bodies, moves all things in time, and links the motions of things that are far apart in place and time. It is also the cause of the fellow-feeling between mortal natures, and of their joining with eternal ones. For the nature in us binds and links all the parts of our body, and it is a kind of fate of the body. In our body some parts lead and others matter less, and the second follow the first. In the same way, in the universe, the comings-to-be of the lesser parts follow the motions of the greater parts: the births below the moon follow the cycles of the heavenly bodies, and the cycle of the first is an image of the second.

flags.taylor: Hence Fate is nature
flags.why: Taylor is following Proclus' treatise On Providence and Fate here; Plato himself does not say that fate is nature.

paragraphs.modern: From this it is not hard to see that providence is God himself, the source of all good. Where else could good come to all things from, if not from the divine? So no other cause of good is to be given, as Plato says, than God. Next, since this cause is above all intelligible and perceptible natures, it is also above fate. Whatever is subject to fate is also ruled by providence: it gets its links from fate, but the good it has from providence. But not everything ruled by providence needs fate, for intelligibles are free of fate's rule. So fate is deeply involved with bodily natures, since linking brings in time and bodily motion. With this in view, Plato says in the Timaeus that the world is mixed from intellect and necessity, intellect ruling over necessity. By necessity here he means the cause that moves bodies, which elsewhere he calls fate. And rightly so, since every body is forced to do whatever it does and suffer whatever it suffers: to heat or be heated, to give or receive cold. A bodily nature knows nothing of choice, so what is necessary and without choice may be called the special marks of bodies.

So, as there are two kinds of things, the intelligible and the perceptible, so there are two kingdoms over them. Above is the kingdom of providence, which reigns over both intelligibles and perceptibles; below is the kingdom of fate, which reigns over perceptibles only. Providence also differs from fate as God differs from what is divine, but by sharing and not in the first place. In other cases we see what exists first and what exists by sharing. The light in the sun is first light, and the light in the air is light by sharing, coming from the first. Life is in the soul first, and in the body second. In the same way, according to Plato, providence is God, but fate is something divine and not a god, for it depends on providence and is, as it were, its image. As providence is to intelligibles, so fate is to perceptibles; and, the other way round, as providence is to fate, so intelligibles are to perceptibles. But intelligibles are the first of beings, and the others get their being from them. So the order of fate depends on the rule of providence.

Second, let us look at the rational nature itself. It corrects the errors of the senses, as when it blames the eye for being deceived in seeing the sun as no wider than a foot. It holds down outbursts of anger, and cries with Odysseus,
"Bear it, my heart."

or it holds back desire when it runs wild after bodily pleasure. In all such work it plainly masters the non-rational motions, both of knowing and of desiring, and frees itself from them as from things foreign to its nature. But we must look for the being of anything not in its distorted state, but in its natural activities. Reason, when it acts in us as reason, holds back the shadowy picture of the pleasures of unruly desire, punishes the rash rush of rage, and rebukes the senses as full of deceit, saying that
"we neither see nor hear anything exactly."

If it says this looking to its inner accounts, none of which it knows through the body or through bodily kinds of knowing, it is clear that in this activity it moves far away from the senses, and, going against their verdict, it separates itself from those pains and pleasures.

Next, let us turn to another and better motion of our rational soul. When the lower parts are quiet, it turns to itself and sees its own being, the powers it holds, the harmonious proportions it is made of, and the many lives of which it is the middle boundary. So it finds itself to be a rational world: an image of the prior natures it comes from, and a pattern of those that come after it. Theoretical arithmetic and geometry help greatly towards this activity of the soul. They take it away from the senses, clean the intellect of the non-rational forms of life that surround it, and lead it to a bodiless perception of the Forms. The soul comes to these sciences full of images, knowing nothing fine, and chattering with matter. If they make clear accounts that have the unbreakable necessity of proof, and forms full of complete certainty, free of matter, which never call on the inexactness of perceptible things for help, do they not plainly clean our life of intellect of the things that fill us with lack of intellect and block our perception of true being?

After both these activities of the rational soul, let us now look at her highest intelligence. By it she sees her sister souls in the universe, which have been given homes in the heavens and in the whole of visible nature by the will of the maker of the world. But above all souls she sees beings and orders of intellect. For a godlike intellect lives above every soul, and gives the soul a habit of intellect. Before these she sees those divine monads from which all the multitudes of intellect get their unions. For above all things that are united there must be causes that unite; above things given life, causes that give life; above natures of intellect, those that give intellect; and above all that share, natures that are not shared. From all these upward ways of understanding it must be plain to anyone not wholly blind how the soul, leaving sense and body behind, looks, through the outreaching activity of intellect, at beings wholly free of any link with bodily nature.

So the rational soul, and the soul of intellect, in whatever way it moves by its nature, is above body and sense. So it must have a being separate from both. And from this again it is clear that, when it acts by its nature, it is above fate and out of reach of its pull. But when it falls into sense and into what is non-rational and made bodily, it follows the lower natures, and lives with them as with drunken neighbours, and then together with them it comes under the rule of fate. For there must be an order of beings that are above fate in their being, but sometimes ranked under it in their state. There are beings, all the natures of intellect, that are set for ever above the laws of fate; and there are others that, in the whole of their life, are placed under the cycles of fate. So the middle term between them must be a nature that is sometimes above fate's rule and sometimes under it. For the procession of bodiless natures has even fewer gaps than that of bodies.

So human free choice, according to Plato, is a rational power of choosing. It desires both the true good and the apparent good, and leads the soul to both. By it the soul rises and falls, goes wrong and acts rightly. So the power of choice is the same as what marks our very being. By this power we differ from divine natures and from mortal ones, for each of these lacks this two-way leaning. The divine, because of its excellence, is set only in the true good; the mortal, because of its lack, only in the apparent good. Intellect marks the first, and sense the second; and the first, as Plotinus says, is our king, and the second our messenger. So we are set in the middle, in the power of choice. We can lean both to the true good and to the apparent good. When we lean to the first, we follow intellect as guide; when to the second, sense. So the power in us cannot do all things. The power that can do everything is marked by unity; it is all-powerful because it is one and has the form of the Good. But the power of choice is double, and so it cannot do all things, because its leaning to the true good and to the apparent good makes it fall short of the nature that comes before all things. It would be all-powerful if it had no impulse of choice and were will alone. For a life that is will alone is a life in the Good, since the will by nature leans to the good; and such a life makes what is most our own most powerful and most like God. Through this, according to Plato, the soul becomes divine, and in another life governs the world together with God. So much for the outline of the leading teachings of Plato's philosophy.

flags.taylor: a rational elective power, desiderative of true and apparent good
flags.why: This account of free choice (proairesis) comes from Proclus, On Providence and Fate; Plato has no single word for it.

paragraphs.modern: At the start of this Introduction I said that, in drawing this outline, I would lead the reader along new and lonely paths. Lonely they must be, since no one has walked them from the reign of the emperor Justinian to the present day. And they will no doubt seem new to readers of every kind, but above all to those who have been brought up, as it were, at the breast of matter: the pupils of experiment, the darlings of the senses, the true descendants of the earth-born giants who made war on the gods of Olympus. They have stared at the dark and ugly face of their nurse until they cannot see the light of truth. They have drunk so deeply from the cup of forgetting, and become so drowsy, that their whole life is only a passing from sleep to sleep and from dream to dream, like men moving from one bed to another. To such people the road we have travelled will seem a false track, and the things we have seen only fantasies, seen by the eye of imagination alone, and, when seen, as empty and idle as the dreams of a shadow.

flags.taylor: they have been unfrequented from the reign of the emperor Justinian to the present time

paragraphs.modern: Still, the following arguments may wake a few of them, less sleepy than the rest, from the sleep of the senses. They may help them lift the mind's eye out of the dark mud they are sunk in, and catch sight of this weightiest truth: that there is another world, of which this one is only a very dim likeness, and another life, of which this one is only a fleeting mockery. So what I say now is addressed to those who think experiment the only firm test of truth.

paragraphs.modern: First, these people seem not to know the fixed laws of proof in the strict sense. The required marks of all propositions used in proof are these: they must be causes of the conclusions, and come first, be better, belong to the subject, be true, and be better known than the conclusions. Every proof is made not only of starting points that come before others, but of starting points that are first in the full sense. If the propositions we assume can be proved from other assumptions, they may seem to come before the conclusions, but they have no right to be called first. Others, on the contrary, need no proof but are plain in themselves, and these are rightly held the first, the truest and the best. The ancients called such unprovable truths axioms, from their dignity and authority, since the assumptions that make up a proof draw all their force from them.

Next, they do not seem to see clearly enough that a universal proof is better than a particular one. The better proof is the one drawn from the better cause, and a universal cause reaches further and is better than a particular one, since the hard search for the "why" of anything stops only when it reaches universals. Suppose we want to know why the outside angles of a triangle add up to four right angles, and the answer is, "Because the triangle is isosceles." We ask again, "But why because it is isosceles?" If the answer is, "Because it is a triangle," we may ask again, "But why because it is a triangle?" Finally we answer, "Because a triangle is a figure with straight sides." Here our inquiry rests at the universal idea, which takes in every particular one before it and is held by no idea more general than itself. Add that a proof about particulars is almost a proof about an endless number of things, while a proof about universals is a proof about a limited number; and of the endless there can be no knowledge. Also, the best proof is the one that gives the mind the widest knowledge, and only universals do this. We may add that whoever knows universals also knows particulars in potential; but we cannot infer that whoever knows particulars best knows anything of universals. Lastly, the universal is the object of intellect and reason, while particulars belong with the perceptions of sense.

Here, perhaps, the experimenter will say: "Grant all this. Still, we get sight of these universals only by induction from particulars and by abstraction from perceptible things." My answer is that the universal which is the proper object of knowledge is not at all the child of abstraction; induction serves its coming into being only as something that stirs it up. If the conclusions of knowledge are beyond doubt, and if the truth of proof is necessary and eternal, this universal is truly all, and not, like the universal gained by abstraction, limited to a certain number of particulars. Take the proposition that the angles of every triangle add up to two right angles. If it is certainly true, that is, if "every" really includes all triangles, it cannot be the result of any abstraction. Abstraction, however wide, is limited, and falls far short of taking in everything. Then how does discursive reason conclude so confidently that the proposition is true of all triangles? Someone may say that the mind, after abstracting "triangle" from a certain number of particulars, adds from itself what is missing to complete the "all." But first, no one, I think, will say that anything like this happened in his mind when he first learned this proposition. And second, if we granted it, the proposition would be a mere fiction, since it would be uncertain whether what is added to complete the "all" is truly added; and so the conclusion would no longer be certainly necessary.

In short, if the words "all" and "every," which fill every page of theoretical mathematics, mean what everyone takes them to mean, and if the universals they stand for are the proper objects of knowledge, then such universals must exist in the soul before the senses act. So induction serves knowledge only by making axioms and postulates believable, and it does this by stirring up the universal ideas of them that lie hidden in the soul. So the particulars from which an induction is made, in order to produce knowledge, must be so simple that they can be grasped at once, and that the universal can be said of them without hesitation. The particulars of the experimenters are not of this kind, and so they can never be sources of knowledge in the true sense.

The experimenter seems to know nothing of this. And so he also does not know that parts can only be truly known through wholes. This is above all true of parts that belong to a whole which, as we have said, holds within itself the parts it produces, and is therefore called a whole before its parts. No one would deserve the name of doctor who tried to cure any part of the human body without first knowing the whole. In the same way, no one can know anything truly about the plant life of plants who does not first know the plant life that exists in the earth as a whole, which comes before all particular plant life because it is its principle and cause; and who does not know, before that, the still greater whole of this kind that exists in nature herself. Nor, as Hippocrates rightly says, can anyone know anything truly about the nature of the human body who does not know what nature is, taken as a great all-embracing whole. If this is true of all inquiries into nature, and it most certainly is, how much more must it be true of knowing those bodiless forms to which we climbed in the first part of this Introduction! Since they come from wholes wholly free of body, body shares in them much more dimly and imperfectly. Here, then, is the great difference, and a mighty one, between knowledge gained by the most careful experiments and knowledge gained by reasoning that rests on the natural, undistorted, self-shining ideas of the soul. The first does not even lead its follower up to the one nature of the earth, from which, as from an ever-living root, flower the natures of all the animals and plants on its surface and of all the minerals and metals inside it. The second leads its follower through all the wholes of the world up to that great whole, the world itself, and from there through the bright order of bodiless wholes to that vast whole of wholes in which all other wholes are centred and rooted, which is nothing else than the principle of all principles and the source of the divine itself. The difference in where the two pursuits lead is just as striking. One raises the soul to the brightest heights, and to that great inexpressible which is beyond all height. The other brings the soul great harm since, in Plutarch's fine phrase, it puts out her chief and brightest eye, the knowledge of God. In short, one leads to all that is grand, high and splendid in the universe; the other to all that is small, crawling and dark. One is the parent of the purest and most ardent devotion; the true children of the other are impiety and atheism. And, finally, one gives its follower the most sincere, lasting and lofty joy; the other, constant disappointment and endless trouble.

If these are the results and tendencies of experimental inquiries, when they are pursued as the test of truth, and daily experience sadly shows that they are, there can be no cure for this great evil except the philosophy of intellect taught by Plato. The good tendency of this philosophy is so plain that its author has been called "divine" by everyone for more than two thousand years. And it stands so high that it can be shown without much trouble that the greatest men of antiquity, from the time its healing light first blessed the human race, have all been more or less filled with its holy principles and devoted to its divine truths. To name a few out of a countless crowd: among rulers it had Dion of Syracuse, the Roman emperor Julian and the Persian king Khosrow; among generals, Chabrias and Phocion, those brave commanders of the Athenians; among mathematicians, those leading stars of knowledge, Eudoxus, Archimedes and Euclid; among biographers, the matchless Plutarch; among doctors, the admirable Galen; among orators, those unrivalled speakers Demosthenes and Cicero; among critics, that prince of scholars, Longinus; and among poets, the most learned and majestic Virgil. After the fall of the Roman empire, examples that come near these in brightness, though not equal to them, can no doubt be given. But they were formed on these great ancients as models, and so they are only streams from Platonic rivers. Examples of philosophical achievement equal to those among the Greeks might have been found among the moderns too, if the hand of barbarous tyranny had not forced philosophy to withdraw into the deepest solitude, by pulling down her schools and wrapping the human intellect in deepest darkness. In our own country, though no one seems to have given himself wholly to the study of this philosophy (and whoever does not will never reach its depths), we have a few bright examples of uncommon skill in its easier parts. I mean Shaftesbury, Akenside, Harris, Petvin and Sydenham. These writers showed such splendid gifts for philosophy, like the fair dawn of a cloudless morning, that we can only deeply regret that the sun of their genius set before it gladdened us with its full brightness. Had it shone with its full strength, the writer of this Introduction would not have tried either to translate Plato's works or to explain his teachings. But though it rose strongly, it did not scatter the clouds that slowly covered its light, and the eye waited anxiously, and in vain, for its noonday beam.

paragraphs.modern: In short, the principles of Plato's philosophy are, of all others, the most friendly to true devotion, pure morals, solid learning and sound government. For it is founded on real knowledge in all its parts, and these parts take in all that a human being can know in theology and ethics, and all he needs to know about nature. So it must hold within itself the source of all that is great and good for individuals and for communities. It must raise while it helps, and make divine while it raises.

We have said that this philosophy first shone out through Plato with a hidden and holy brightness. Because he gave it in a hidden way, its depth was not sounded until many ages after he taught it; and when it was sounded, shallow readers met it with mockery and contempt. Plato was not alone in teaching his philosophy in a hidden way. This was the custom of all the great ancients. It did not come from a wish to rule over knowledge like tyrants and keep the many in ignorance, but from a deep conviction that the highest truths are profaned when they are laid out plainly to the crowd. And this must follow, since, as Socrates rightly says in Plato, "it is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure"; and the many are cleansed neither of the stains of vice nor of the darkness of double ignorance (not knowing, and not knowing that they do not know). So while they are doubly impure, they can no more see the brightness of truth than an eye buried in mud can see the light of day.

So the depth of this philosophy seems not to have been fully reached, except by Plato's own pupils, for more than five hundred years after it was first taught. Crantor, Atticus, Albinus, Galen and Plutarch were men of great gifts, and made uncommon progress in philosophy. Yet they do not seem to have brought out the depth of Plato's thought. They did not draw back the veil over his hidden meaning, like the curtains that kept the inner shrine of a temple from unholy eyes, and they did not see that behind the veil all is bright, and divine sights appear on every side. This task was kept for men born in a lower age, who had a nature like their leader's and were the true interpreters of his hidden thought. The most famous of them are the great Plotinus, the most learned Porphyry, the divine Iamblichus, the most acute Syrianus, Proclus the crown of philosophical excellence, the splendid Hierocles, the briefly elegant Sallustius, and the most searching Damascius. By these men, true links in the golden chain of the divine, all that is high and all that is hidden in Plato's teachings (and these are full of both, beyond measure) was freed from darkness and brought into the most pleasing and admirable light. But their labours have been met with ingratitude. The beautiful light they kindly brought out has, unnoticed till now, lit philosophy in her empty retreats, like a lamp shining on a revered statue among dark and lonely ruins. What the master foretold has sadly come true of these, his best pupils:

So, as for these admirable men, the last and truest of Plato's followers: some readers know nothing of Plato's hidden teachings, and find these interpreters full of ideas that are not plain to everyone in Plato's writings. So they at once conclude that such ideas are mere jargon and daydreams, not truly Platonic, only streams that came from a pure spring but have been fouled by their distance from it. Others care only for the finest purity of language, and look down on every writer who lived after the fall of the Macedonian empire; as if dignity and weight of thought could not be had without splendid and exact wording, or as if fine writers could not exist in a lower age. This is far from true. Although the style of Plotinus and Iamblichus cannot be compared with Plato's, its weakness is lost in the depth and height of their thought, and a thoughtful reader pays as little attention to it as the eye, gladly turning to the sun, pays to the specks of dust in a sunbeam.

As for Porphyry's style: he was the pupil of Longinus, whom Eunapius neatly calls "a living library and a walking museum," so it is only reasonable to suppose that he took in some of his master's skill in writing. That he did is clear from Eunapius' witness, who praises his style especially for its clearness, purity and grace. "So," he says, "Porphyry, let down to men like a chain of Hermes, made everything clear and pure through his wide learning." And elsewhere he speaks of him as full of every grace of style, and as the only one who showed and proclaimed his master's praise. The style of Proclus is pure, clear and elegant, like that of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, but much fuller and grander. That of Hierocles is solemn and majestic, almost equal to the style of the greatest ancients. That of Sallustius has an exactness and a pregnant brevity that can hardly be told apart from the writing of Aristotle. And lastly, the style of Damascius is clear and exact, and well worthy of a most searching mind.

Others again have filled themselves with empty confidence from reading the commentaries of these admirable interpreters, and in a short time have thought themselves better than their masters. So it was with Ficino, Pico, Dr Henry More and other false Platonists of their time. To join Christianity with Plato's teachings, they rejected some of his most important beliefs and twisted others. So they spoiled one of these systems and did the other no real good.

Was it because that bishop and sophist, Warburton, chose to talk about "the polluted streams of the Alexandrian school" without knowing anything of the spring those streams come from? Or because some dull German critic, who knew nothing beyond the grammar of a Greek verb, dared to grunt at these revered heroes? Whatever its source and whenever it began (I have not been able to find out either), one thing is certain: it owes its existence to the deepest ignorance or the most cunning sophistry, and its origin is as contemptible as it is obscure. Let us consider for a moment the advantages these later Platonists had over any of their modern critics. First, Greek was their native language. Since they were learned men, as all agree, they must have understood it far better than anyone since ancient Greek was a living language. Second, they had books to consult, written by Plato's own pupils, which have been lost for more than a thousand years, and many Pythagorean writings, from which Plato himself took most of his higher teachings. So these excellent interpreters constantly quote the works of Parmenides, Empedocles, Zeno of Elea, Speusippus, Xenocrates and many other famous philosophers of the earliest times, who were either true Platonists or the sources of Platonism. Third, they joined the greatest gifts to the most untiring effort, and the greatest purity of life to the sharpest strength of intellect. Consider, too, that the philosophy to which these great men gave their lives was openly taught by its author in a hidden way; that Aristotle himself studied it for twenty years; and that, as Plato tells us in one of his Letters, it was not unusual to find students who could not understand its highest teachings in an even longer time. When we consider all this, what must we think of the arrogance, not to say the impudence, of people in the seventeenth, eighteenth and nineteenth centuries who have dared to slander these great masters of wisdom? People for whom Greek is not a native language; who have no such books to consult as those they abuse; who have never dreamed of making the gaining of wisdom the great aim of their lives; and who, in short, have made that most harmful mistake of taking the study of words for philosophy, and words for things?
