But it is time now to give the reader a general view of Plato's works, and to speak of the openings, the digressions and the style of their author, and of the translation that follows. For the first of these I will use the Synopsis of Mr Sydenham, taking the liberty to correct it where it seems wrong and to add to it where it seems to fall short.

Plato's dialogues are of various kinds, not only in the different matters they deal with, but also in the way they are composed or built, and in the form in which they appear to the reader. So it will not be out of place, I think, to follow the advice Plato himself gives in the Phaedrus, and the example of the ancient Platonists, and to sort them into kinds: first dividing them into the most general kinds, then dividing these into lesser ones, until we reach the lowest kinds, which show exactly the nature of each dialogue and from which each should take its name.

The most general division of Plato's writings is into those that question and those that teach. In the first, nothing is plainly proved or stated. Some philosophical question is only looked at and examined, and the reader is left to draw the conclusions and find the truths the philosopher means to suggest. This is done either by inquiry or by argument and dispute. By argument proceed all the dialogues meant to root out false opinions. They do this either indirectly, by tangling those opinions in difficulties and putting their holders at a loss, or directly, by refuting them. By inquiry proceed those meant to raise right opinions in the mind. They do this either by spurring the reader on to pursue some part of wisdom and showing how to search for it, or by leading the way and helping the mind forward in the search. This is done by working through opposing arguments.

The dialogues of the other kind, the teaching ones, teach some point of doctrine openly. They do this either by laying it down on authority or by proving it with reasons and arguments. On authority, the doctrine is given sometimes by the speaker himself, as a master, and at other times as handed down to him from wise men. The method of teaching by argument or proof that Plato uses works in all the ways of dialectic: dividing, defining, proving and analysing. Its aim is the search for truth alone.
This division gives the following table:

DIALOGUES
  Questioning: arguing (putting at a loss; refuting) or inquiring (spurring on; helping)
  Teaching: proving (by analysis; by induction) or on authority (as a master; from tradition)
(Taylor sets this out as a branching table.)

In varying his manner like this, and dividing his writings into these kinds, the philosopher does not mean only to entertain us with variety. Nor does he mean to teach more or less plainly on different occasions, or to suggest that some teachings are more certain than others. He works this way as a perfect master of the art of writing in dialogue. From the different characters of the speakers, as from different elements in the make-up of these dramatic dialogues, or different ingredients in their mixture, he produces a special spirit and temper, as it were, in each.

Socrates is the main speaker in almost all of them. But when he meets some arrogant sophist, and the modest wisdom and clear knowledge of the one are set against the confident ignorance and blind conceit of the other, dispute and controversy naturally follow, and the false pretender is bound to be either puzzled or refuted. Just to puzzle him is enough if no one else is present, because such a man can never be refuted in his own opinion. But when there is an audience round them, in danger of being led into error by sophistry, then the true philosopher must do his utmost, and the vain sophist must be convicted and exposed.

In some dialogues Plato shows his great master talking with young men of the best families in the city. When these have teachable natures and fair minds, the philosopher has the chance to call out the hidden seeds of wisdom and to grow these noble plants with true teaching, in the friendly, familiar way of looking into things together. This gives such dialogues their spirit of inquiry. There, through a seeming equality in the conversation, the curiosity or eagerness of a mere stranger is stirred, that of a pupil is encouraged, and, by the right questions, the mind is helped forward in its search for truth.

At other times the philosophical hero of these dialogues appears in a higher role, talking with men of better-trained understanding and more enlightened minds. Then he has the chance to teach more openly and to show the reasons of things, for to such an audience the truth is owed, and every kind of proof is possible in teaching it. So the dialogues with these speakers naturally take on the spirit of argument and proof, using, as we said before, all the methods of dialectic.

But when the teaching cannot be proved, he takes on an air of authority. Such is the teaching about ancient times, which is only handed down and is a matter of belief; and such is the teaching about laws, which is commanded and is a matter of obedience. In the first case the teaching is handed on from the authority of ancient sages; in the second it is laid down as a master, with the authority of a lawgiver.

So much for the way Plato's dialogues are each composed, and the spirit their composition gives them. The form in which they appear, the outward mark that sets them apart, is of three sorts. They are either purely dramatic, like the dialogue of a tragedy or comedy; or purely narrated, where an earlier conversation is supposed to be written down and sent to an absent friend; or mixed, like the tellings in dramatic poems, where the story of past events is told to someone present.

We have divided Plato's dialogues by the inner form, or make-up, that gives them their spirit, and by the outer form that marks them with a character, as flowers and other plants are marked. Next we must divide them by their subject and their aim, beginning with their aim, since the subjects are all chosen for its sake. The aim of all Plato's writings is the aim of all true philosophy or wisdom: the perfection and happiness of human beings. So the human being is the general subject. The first business of philosophy must be to ask what this being we call human is, who is to be made happy, and what his nature is, in whose perfection his happiness lies. But since we have tried, in the earlier part of this Introduction, to outline Plato's teaching about the human being, there is no need to say more about it here.

So Plato's dialogues may be divided, by their subjects, into the theoretical, the practical and the mixed. The subjects of the mixed are either general, taking in both the others, or distinguishing, telling them apart. The general subjects are either foundational or final. The foundational are philosophy, human nature and the human soul; the final are love, beauty and the good. The distinguishing subjects concern knowledge in its relation to practice, and in them two questions are considered: whether virtue can be taught, and whether going wrong in the will depends on going wrong in judgment. The subjects of the theoretical dialogues concern either words or things. Of the first sort are the origins of words, sophistry, rhetoric and poetry; of the second, knowledge, true being, the principles of mind, and outward nature. The practical subjects concern either private conduct, and the rule of the mind over the whole person; or one's duty to others in one's various relationships; or the government of a state and the public conduct of a whole people. Under these three heads come, in order, the particular practical subjects: virtue in general, holiness, self-control and courage; justice, friendship, love of country and piety; the ruling mind in a state, the form and order of a state, law in general, and lastly the rules of government and public conduct, the civil laws.

So, to give the reader a view of Plato's writings that is rigorous, that is, both complete and clearly divided, we have tried to show their proper, natural divisions, whether the reader looks at them by their inner form or essence, their outer form or appearance, their matter, or their end; or, in the plainer words we have used in this Synopsis, by their spirit, their character, their subject and their aim.

We should note here that it is the mark of the highest good to do good to everything, though some things gain more from it and others less, as they are more or less fit to receive it. In the same way, Plato's dialogues are so deeply stamped with the marks of the highest good that they do some good even to those who cannot reach their depths. They can tame a savage sophist, like Thrasymachus in the Republic. They can humble the arrogance even of those who do not know their own ignorance. They can make people skilled in political virtue who will never reach the virtue of contemplation. In short, like the light that comes from God, wherever those who receive them are at all fit for it, they purify, light up and raise.

After this general view of Plato's dialogues, let us next consider their openings, the digressions they are full of, and the character of their style. As for the openings, however needless they may seem at first sight, a closer look shows that they are necessary to the aim of the dialogues they begin. So the opening part of the Timaeus sets out the account of the world in images, as the Pythagoreans did. And the first part of the Parmenides, the discussion of Forms, is really only an opening to the second part, the study of the One, for which it is an essential preparation. So, as Plutarch says when he speaks of Plato's dialogue about the island of Atlantis, these openings are grand gates and splendid courtyards with which he deliberately adorns his great buildings, so that nothing may be lacking to their beauty and all may be equally splendid. He acts, as Dacier rightly says, like a great prince who, when he builds a rich palace, adorns its entrance (in Pindar's words) with golden pillars. For what is seen first should be splendid and grand, and should clearly announce, as it were, all the grandeur that will be seen afterwards.

As for the many digressions in his dialogues, a careful look shows that they too serve the main aim of the dialogues they appear in, while they also give the mind a pleasant rest from the labour of hard inquiry. So Plato, by a most happy and charming art, leads the reader to the temple of Truth through the delightful groves and valleys of the Graces. In short, this winding road, looked at carefully, is the shortest road by which he could lead the reader to the end he wants. For in doing this we must look not at the road that is straightest in the nature of things, taken in the abstract, but at the one that is most direct for the way human understanding moves forward.

As for Plato's style, it is really the least part of the worth of his writings, since in all works of philosophy style should be the last thing attended to. Yet even here Plato can compete for the prize with the most famous masters of language. So his style was admired by the finest writers of antiquity. According to Ammianus, Zeus himself would speak no differently if he talked in Attic Greek. Aristotle thought his style halfway between poetry and prose. Cicero praises him no less for the excellence of his language than for the depth of his thought; and Longinus calls him, in his language, the rival of Homer. So that prince of critics sees him as drawing many streams from the spring of Homer into himself, and compares him, in his rivalry with Homer, to a new challenger entering the contest against one whom all already admire.

Yet despite this praise Plato has been accused, as Longinus tells us, of often being carried away, as if by a Bacchic frenzy of words, into excessive and unpleasant metaphors and an allegorical grandeur of language. Longinus excuses this by saying that whatever is naturally great has very little of the flawless, since what is exact in every way risks being small. He adds:

"And may this not also be necessary: that people of low and middling talent, because they never take risks or aim at the summit of excellence, are mostly free of faults and stay safe, while great things are unsafe because of their very greatness?"

It seems to me that whenever this overflowing, this Bacchic frenzy, appears in Plato's language, it is because of the greatness of the divine inspiration that fills him at the time. That he sometimes wrote from divine inspiration is clear from his own words in the Phaedrus, a great part of which is less like an orderly speech than a dithyrambic poem. Such a style, born of divine madness, which, as Plato rightly says, is better than all human good sense, naturally takes on the shape of its cause. It imitates a power above nature, as far as words can, and so it must be grand, forceful and overflowing, since those are the marks of its source. But all judges of writing, ancient and modern, agree that his style is in general graceful and pure, and that it is high without being violent and rushed. It is as harmonious as it is lofty, as exact as it is grand. It joins the force of the greatest orators to the graces of the first of poets. In short, it is a river to which those well-known lines of Denham may most fittingly be applied:

Though deep, yet clear; though gentle, yet not dull;
strong without rage; without overflowing, full.

We have now considered Plato's philosophy, given a general view of his writings, and made some remarks on his style. It only remains to speak of the order of the dialogues that follows, and of the translation of his works, and then to close this Introduction with a few fitting remarks.

Since no exact and rigorous order of these dialogues has come down to us from the ancients, I had to make one of my own. I trust it is not unrigorous, however inferior it may be to the order that the later interpreters of Plato surely made, though it is sadly lost. In my order I have imitated the order of the universe, in which, as I have said, wholes come before parts and universals before particulars. So I have put first the dialogues that are wholes, or form a system, and after them those in which these systems branch out into particulars. So after the First Alcibiades, which may be called, and which the ancients seem generally to have thought, an introduction to the whole of Plato's philosophy, I have put the Republic and the Laws, which may be said to contain Plato's ethics and politics as a system. After these comes the Timaeus, which contains the whole of his study of nature, and with it the Critias, because it is linked to the Timaeus. Next is the Parmenides, which contains a system of his theology. Up to this point the order follows the natural progress of the human mind in gaining the highest knowledge. The order after this mainly follows the order of things. So after the Parmenides come the Sophist, the Phaedrus, the Greater Hippias and the Symposium. These may be seen as lesser wholes, under and held within the Parmenides, which, like the universe itself, is a whole of wholes. For in the Sophist being itself is studied, in the Symposium love itself, and in the Phaedrus beauty itself; all these are intelligible Forms, and so are held in the Parmenides, in which the whole range of the intelligible is set out. The Greater Hippias is put with the Phaedrus because the whole series of the beautiful is discussed in the second, and the beauty that exists in soul in the first. After these comes the Theaetetus, which studies knowledge as it exists in the soul; knowledge itself, as it first exists, having already been praised by Socrates in one part of the Phaedrus. The Statesman and the Minos, which come next, may be seen as branches of the Laws. In short, all the dialogues that follow either look more closely at the teachings held as a system in those already listed, or flow naturally from them as their source. Since it did not seem possible to arrange the dialogues that are parts in the same exact order as those we took as wholes, it seemed better to group them either by their agreement in some one feature, as the Phaedo, the Apology and the Crito, which all concern the death of Socrates, and the Meno and the Protagoras, which concern whether virtue can be taught; or by their agreement in character, as the Lesser Hippias and the Euthydemus, which overturn opinions, and the Theages, the Laches and the Lysis, which bring ideas to birth. The Cratylus is put last, not so much because its subject is the origin of words, as because a great part of it is deeply theological. By this order, after climbing in the Parmenides to all the divine orders and their inexpressible principle, and coming down from there step by step to the human soul in the dialogues that follow, the reader is led back again to the divine in this dialogue. So he imitates the order that all beings keep, that of always returning to the principles they flow from.

flags.taylor: no accurate and scientific arrangement then of these dialogues has been transmitted to us from the ancients
flags.why: Taylor overlooks the order of Iamblichus' curriculum, which the Anonymous Prolegomena (26) hands down; the Workshop lists the dialogues in that order.

paragraphs.modern: After the dialogues come Plato's Letters, which are in every way worthy of that prince of all true philosophers. They are written not only with great elegance, and at times with grandeur of language, but with all the fitting dignity of a mind aware of its high gifts, and with all the authority of a master of philosophy. They are also full of admirable remarks on politics, and contain some of his most hidden teachings. Though these are given in riddles, the way they are given both throws light on what is said of these teachings in his more theological dialogues and is lit up by it.

flags.taylor: which are in every respect worthy that prince of all true philosophers
flags.why: Most modern scholars think that most or all of the Letters are not by Plato; the ancient Platonists accepted them.

paragraphs.modern: As for the translation that follows, I must first point out that Plato's genuine dialogues number fifty-five. Although the Republic is one work and the Laws another, the first has ten books and the second twelve, and each of these books is a dialogue. Since there are thirty-three dialogues besides the Laws and the Republic, the whole comes to fifty-five, as we said. Of these fifty-five, Mr Sydenham translated the following nine: the First and Second Alcibiades, the Greater and Lesser Hippias, the Symposium (except Alcibiades' speech), the Philebus, the Meno, the Ion and the Lovers. I have already said, with deep regret, that this excellent but unlucky scholar died before he had made the progress in Plato's philosophy that might reasonably have been expected from so fine a start. I knew him personally only at the end of his life, when his mind had not only been much weakened by age but badly harmed by misfortune. His life had been very stormy. For many years before his death he was poor; his patrons were far from generous; and his true friends were neither many nor rich. He began to study Plato, as he told me himself, when he was well past the middle of life, and with most unfortunate prejudices against Plato's best followers. I tried to remove these while I knew him, and partly succeeded, but illness and death stopped me finishing. In such circumstances it was not to be expected that he would sound the depths of Plato's thought and reach the summit of philosophy. But I saw that his gifts and his natural temper might have ranked him among the best interpreters of Plato, if he had not given way under misfortune, if he had not nursed such harmful prejudices, and if he had not neglected philosophy early in life. Had that happened, my labours would have been much lighter, or perhaps not needed at all, and his name would have been handed down with lasting fame. Since sadly it did not happen, I have had to examine closely, and compare with the Greek, all those parts of the dialogues he translated that are more deeply philosophical or contain anything of Plato's theology. In these, as might be expected, I found him badly lacking. Sometimes he mistook the meaning through ignorance of Plato's higher teachings, and at other times he twisted it to suit some opinions of his own. But his translation of the other, less difficult parts is excellent. In these he gives the reader faithfully not only the matter of Plato but his true manner too. And the notes that go with these parts generally show sound criticism and wide learning, fine taste and a naturally philosophical mind. I have kept as many of these notes as the size and plan of this work allowed.

flags.taylor: the number of the legitimate dialogues of Plato is fifty-five
flags.why: Taylor's count follows the ancient Thrasyllan list; many of the works he counts (the Second Alcibiades, the Lovers, the Theages, the Minos) are now thought not to be by Plato.

paragraphs.modern: Of the translation of the Republic by Dr Spens, I must say that much of it is very faithful, but that in the harder parts it is inexact, and that it is everywhere full of Scotticisms that offend an English ear and vulgarisms that disgrace the translator as much as they disgust the reader. It is enough to say of this version that I have used it wherever I found I properly could, and given my own translation where I could not.

Of the ten dialogues translated by Dacier I can say nothing exactly, because I know no French at all. But if one may judge this work from an English translation of it, I will say boldly that it is far from literal and very often mistakes the sense of the Greek. So I could get little help from it; some I did get, and that little I gladly acknowledge. In translating the rest of Plato's works, which, as the reader can easily see, is by far the greater part of them, I have had help from no translation except Ficino's. Every student of Plato knows how good it generally is. This comes not only from his knowing Platonism better than any translator after him, but also from his having made it from a very valuable manuscript in the Medici library that can no longer be found. I have, however, used the learned work of the editors of various dialogues: Forster's edition of the Lovers, Euthyphro, Apology, Crito and Phaedo; Etwall's of the First and Second Alcibiades and the Hipparchus; the edition of the Meno, First Alcibiades, Phaedo and Phaedrus printed at Vienna in 1784; Fischer's of the Cratylus and Theaetetus; Massey's of the Republic; and Dr Routh's, President of Magdalen College, Oxford, of the Euthydemus and Gorgias. This last editor has enriched his edition of these two dialogues with very valuable and full notes on language and text, in which he shows as much judgment as learning and as much taste as sharpness. He seems to me one of the best and most modest of scholars, and it is to be hoped that later editors of Plato's text will follow his example.

If my translation had been made with an eye to the judgment of the many, I would have had to apologise for its word-for-word exactness. Had I wanted to please a false taste in writing, I would no doubt have paid less attention to the exact meaning of the Greek. I would have left out almost all the joining words, broken long sentences into many short ones, and split the strong, deep river of Plato's language into smooth, shallow, feeble streams. But this work was written in the hope of helping all, yet with an eye only to the judgment of men of high souls. So I have tried not to lose a word of the Greek, and at the same time to give the translation as much elegance as such exactness of words allows. I have also tried to keep the manner as well as the matter of my author, being fully convinced that no translation deserves praise in which both are not kept as far as possible.

flags.taylor: have divided long periods into a number of short ones
flags.why: The Workshop's modern version does just what Taylor refused to do here, breaking his long sentences into short ones; his own words are always one tap away.

paragraphs.modern: My main aim in this hard undertaking has been to bring out all Plato's hidden and high teachings, as they are found scattered through his works. To unravel in detail the art he uses in writing all his dialogues, and to do full justice to his meaning in every point, must be the work of someone with more leisure, who can publish Plato's works on a larger plan. To reach my aim, I have given the reader in my notes almost the whole substance, in English, of all the following Greek commentaries and notes on Plato that exist only in manuscript: Proclus' commentaries on the Parmenides and the First Alcibiades, and his notes on the Cratylus; Olympiodorus' notes on the Phaedo, Gorgias and Philebus; and Hermias' on the Phaedrus. To these are added very full extracts from the manuscript of Damascius, On First Principles (Peri Archōn), and from the published works of Proclus on the Timaeus, the Republic and the Theology of Plato. Of the first four of these manuscripts, three of which are large folio volumes, I have complete copies made with my own hand. Of the full extracts from the others, those from Olympiodorus on the Gorgias I took from the copy kept in the British Museum; those from the same philosopher on the Philebus, and those from Hermias on the Phaedrus and Damascius' On First Principles, from the copies in the Bodleian Library.

Here gratitude requires me to thank publicly the University of Oxford, and the chief librarian and assistant librarians of the Bodleian Library, for the generous and kind way they received me while I was making these extracts. First, I must thank Dr Jackson, Dean of Christ Church, for his very courteous attention. Second, the freedom to work in the Bodleian, and the help given me there by the librarians of that excellent collection, deserve no small praise. Above all, the generous welcome I had from the fellows of New College, with whom I stayed for three weeks and from whom I received a truly Greek hospitality, will, I trust, be as hard for time to wipe from my memory as it is for me to express it as it deserves.

As for the faults I may have made in this translation (for I am not so vain as to think it has none), I might plead in excuse that the whole of it was done while I suffered badly from ill health and poverty, and that a large part of it was done amid other troubles of no common size, and other labours that worked against such a task. But whatever my mistakes, I will not hide behind misfortune for an excuse. Let my excuse be this: whatever mistakes I may have made in smaller points came from my eagerness to grasp and to spread those great truths of Plato's philosophy and theology. Though they have been hidden and forgotten for ages, they are as old as the universe, and they will be brought back again and will flourish for very long periods, through all the endless cycles of time.

Next I must speak of what a true student of Plato's philosophy needs. Before that, I will just point out how absurd it is to suppose that a knowledge of Greek alone, however great, is enough to understand Plato's high teachings. One might as well think one could understand Archimedes without knowing the elements of geometry, just because one can read him in Greek. Those who hold such an idle opinion would do well to think about the deep saying of Heraclitus, that "much learning does not teach intellect" (Polumathiē noon ou didaskei).

flags.taylor: polymathy does not teach intellect
flags.why: Heraclitus' word noos here means "understanding" or "sense"; "intellect" is Taylor's Platonist rendering, kept for the sake of the key term.

paragraphs.modern: By a true student of the Platonic philosophy, then, I mean someone fitted for so hard a task by both nature and education. Such a person has a naturally good character, is wise and sharp, and burns with a strong desire to gain wisdom and truth. From childhood he has been well taught in mathematics. Besides this he has spent whole days, and often most of the night, in deep thought. Like someone sailing in triumph over a raging sea, or cutting skilfully through an army of enemies, he has met and overcome a hostile crowd of doubts. In short, he has never thought wisdom a thing of small worth and easy to reach, but something that cannot be gained without the most generous and severe endurance, and whose real worth surpasses every bodily good far more than the ocean surpasses the passing bubble on its surface. Then there are those who lack these qualities. They make the study of words their only work, and the pursuit of wisdom at best a side matter. They expect to become wise by dipping into it for an hour or two a day, after the tiring business of the day, after mixing with the low crowd of mankind, laughing with the merry, putting on a serious air with the serious, quietly agreeing with everyone's opinion however absurd, and winking at folly however shameful and low. To these, and sadly the world is full of them, the highest truths must seem only jargon and daydreams, the visions of a sick imagination, or the frothing of a fanatical faith.

But none of this is surprising if we remember that double ignorance is the disease of the many. They are not only ignorant of the highest knowledge; they are ignorant even of their ignorance. So they never suspect their lack of understanding, but at once reject a teaching that seems absurd at first sight, because it is too bright for their bat-like eyes to look at. Or if they do agree that it is true, their very agreement comes from the same dreadful disease of the soul. For they will imagine, says Plato, that they understand the highest truths when the opposite is really the case. So I earnestly beg people of this kind not to meddle with any of the deep inquiries of the Platonic philosophy. It is more dangerous to push them into such work than to advise them to follow their sordid trades without tiring, and to toil for money with ever more eagerness and energy. In this way they will give free rein to the low habits of their soul, and sooner undergo the punishment that in such people must always come before the mind is lit up, and that is the certain result of guilt. Lysis the Pythagorean says well that to teach free inquiries and discussions to people whose morals are muddy and confused is as absurd as to pour pure, clear water into a deep well full of mud and clay; whoever does this only stirs up the mud and fouls the clean water. The thickets of such people, as the same writer finely says (that is, the non-rational, bodily life), in which these dreadful passions are fed, must first be cleared with fire and sword and every kind of tool (that is, through preparatory studies and the political virtues), and reason must be freed from its slavery to the feelings, before anything useful can be planted in these wild places.

flags.taylor: It is well said indeed by Lysis, the Pythagorean
flags.why: The "Letter of Lysis to Hipparchus" that Taylor quotes is a later Pythagorean writing, not by the early Pythagorean Lysis.

paragraphs.modern: So let such people not presume to explore the lands of the Platonic philosophy. The country is too pure to let in the sordid and the low. The road to it is too winding to be found by the unskilled and the dull, and the journey is too long and hard for the soft and the timid, the slave of passion and the dupe of opinion, the lover of the senses and the scorner of truth. The dangers and difficulties of the venture are such that only the toughest and most able adventurers can bear them. Whoever begins the journey without the strength of Heracles, or the wisdom and patience of Odysseus, will be torn apart by the wild beasts of the forest or drown in the storms of the ocean. He will be turned into a beast by the magic of Circe, or kept in exile for life by the spell of Calypso. In short, he must go down into Hades and wander in its darkness without coming out again into the bright lands of morning, or be destroyed by the deadly song of the Sirens. Even to the most skilful traveller, who follows the right road with an eagerness no labour can weaken, a watchfulness no weariness can catch off guard, and a virtue no temptation can lead astray, it looks for many years like the Ithaca of Odysseus or the ever-retreating Italy of Aeneas. No sooner do we catch sight of the pleasant land that is to be the end of our journey than it is suddenly snatched from our view, and we find ourselves still far from the beloved shore, at the mercy of a stormy sea of doubts.

So give up this useless plan, you crawling souls! Run eagerly along the beaten road to popular honours and sordid gain, but drop every thought of a voyage for which you are wholly unprepared. Do you not see what a stretch of sea lies between you and the royal shore? A sea

huge, dreadful, vast, where hardly sails in safety
the best-built ship, though Zeus should send the winds.
(Homer's Odyssey, in an English verse translation.)
And may we not rightly ask you, as Calypso asked,

What ships have you, what sailors to take you,
what oars to cut the long, hard way?
(Homer's Odyssey, in an English verse translation.)

I will only add that I have put Olympiodorus' Life of Plato before this translation, rather than the life by Diogenes Laertius, because the first is the work of a most eminent Platonist, and the second of a mere historian who printed without discrimination whatever stories he found in other writers. If the reader puts this short sketch of Plato's life together with what the philosopher says of himself in his Seventh Letter, he will have the most important facts about him that can be had at present.
